import requests

async def main():

        url=BASE_URL,
        private_key=API_KEY_PRIVATE_KEY,
        account_index=ACCOUNT_INDEX,
        api_key_index=API_KEY_INDEX,

if __name__ == "__main__":

# Lighter integration rules

## Sources of truth
- Docs and API reference: https://apidocs.lighter.xyz (index: https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/llms.txt; append .md to any page)
- Signer: https://github.com/elliottech/lighter-go (WASM: wasm/main.go)
- Look things up before writing code. Do not guess endpoint names, parameters or enum values.

## Environments
- Mainnet: https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai, wss://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream, chainId 304
- Testnet: https://testnet.zklighter.elliot.ai, wss://testnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream, chainId 300
- Default to testnet in examples and tests.

## Accounts and keys
- An L1 (Ethereum) address owns one or more integer account indexes (master + sub-accounts).
- API keys are separate from the Ethereum key. Use API key indexes 4–254 (0–3 are reserved).
- Registering an API key (ChangePubKey) requires the L1 wallet signature over `messageToSign`, set as `L1Sig` in tx_info.
- Never hard-code, log or commit private keys. Load them from env/secret storage.
- Never put a shared/server API key in frontend code.
- For read-only use cases, use read-only tokens (`ro:...`), not API keys.

## Numbers
- Prices and sizes are integers: value × 10^decimals, using `price_decimals` / `size_decimals` from GET /api/v1/orderBookDetails for that market.
- Never hard-code market IDs or decimals outside tests.
- Enforce `min_base_amount` and `min_quote_amount`.
- For taker/market orders, `price` is the worst acceptable price (slippage limit).

## Transactions
- Flow: sign locally with the signer → POST /api/v1/sendTx (form-urlencoded: tx_type, tx_info) → confirm via WebSocket or GET /api/v1/tx.
- `code: 200` means accepted, not executed. Always confirm.
- Nonces are per API key and must increase by 1 unless skipNonce=1. Get with GET /api/v1/nextNonce. Serialize sends per key.
- Before re-signing after an unknown outcome, check the tx status and nextNonce; re-signing with a new nonce can place an order twice.
- orderExpiry is unix milliseconds, 5 minutes–30 days ahead; use 0 for IOC orders.
- clientOrderIndex must be unique across all markets and ≤ 2^48−1.
- Batches: max 50 txs (same account + API key), consecutive nonces, tx_types and tx_infos as JSON-encoded strings. Prefer WebSocket jsonapi/sendtxbatch for more than ~15 txs; large REST bodies can be rejected at the CDN edge.

## WASM signer
- All Sign* functions take positional args; the last two are always apiKeyIndex, accountIndex. Pass 0 for unused args, never undefined.
- Check `result.error` on every call.
- Do all HTTP from JavaScript: pass "" as the CreateClient URL and an explicit nonce; never use CheckClient or nonce=-1 from WASM.
- wasm_exec.js must match the Go version that built the .wasm.

## WebSocket
- Send a frame at least every 2 minutes ({"type":"ping"}); reconnect and resubscribe automatically.
- Order book: snapshot then deltas; verify begin_nonce == previous nonce, else resubscribe.
- Private channels need "auth": <token> (token from CreateAuthToken, max 8h).

## Safety
- Ask a human before: mainnet orders, withdrawals, transfers, changing account tier, registering keys.
- Respect rate limits; back off on HTTP 429/405.
Why these rules
Each rule prevents a mistake we see often in integrations: decimals errors, nonce collisions, keys leaking into frontends, and treating
200
as "filled". See
Troubleshooting
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/api-key.title: API keys
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/api-key.content:
You can use API keys to trade and manage your lighter account programmatically. Each API key will be assigned an index, ranging from 0 to 254 - note that indexes
{0,1,2,3}
are reserved for desktop and mobile interfaces.
Each internal account, whether that's a master account or a sub-account, will have its own separate API key index - and each comes with a public & private key, and its own nonce.
Permissions
Property
Value
Scope
One account index (master, sub-account or pool)
Index range
0–254.
0–3 reserved
for Lighter's web/mobile apps. Use 4–254.
Special index 255
"All keys" – only for querying
apikeys
Nonce
Independent per key (see
Core concepts
)
Registration
ChangePubKey
, requires the L1 wallet signature (or an on-chain call)
Can do
Trade, cancel, modify, leverage/margin, sub-accounts, secure withdrawals, same-owner transfers, auth-gated REST and WebSocket reads
Cannot do alone
Transfers to another L1 owner, fast withdrawals, approving an integrator with fees (these also need the L1 signature)
Secure withdrawals only need the API key because they can only go back to the L1 address that created the account. Fast withdrawals and transfers can go to other L1 addresses, so they also need a signature from the wallet's private key. See
When an L1 signature is required
.
List keys on an account:
Shell
curl "https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/apikeys?account_index=123&api_key_index=255"
Authentication
To interact with certain endpoints, you will need to generate an auth token using your API private key. You can do so using our
GO SDK
, the create_auth_token_with_expiry() function in our
Python SDK
, or the WASM signer:
TypeScript
const deadline = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 3600; // unix seconds, max 8h ahead
const { authToken } = check(lighter.CreateAuthToken(deadline, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX));
Each auth token can have a maximum expiry of 8 hours, and it uses the following structure:
{expiry_unix}:{account_index}:{api_key_index}:{random_hex}
. Refresh tokens before they expire.
Use it as:
REST:
Authorization: <token>
header, or the
auth
query parameter where documented.
WebSocket:
"auth": "<token>"
inside the subscribe message.
Authenticating a request also makes it count against your L1 address instead of your IP. See
Rate Limits
.
Read-only Authentication
Using a canonical auth code, you can generate read-only auth tokens - those won't allow placing trades nor request withdrawals (essentially, you won't be able to sign transactions hence initialize a signer client), but you will be able to access auth-gated data via API. Each read-only auth code can have a maximum expiry of 10 years, and a minimum of 1 day. They will use the following structure:
ro:{account_index}:{single|all}:{expiry_unix}:{random_hex}
.
all
covers the master account and its sub-accounts;
single
covers one account index.
You can generate one using the
createToken
endpoint, or
via front-end
.
tokens/create
is expensive: it costs
23,000
request weight, nearly a full minute of a Plus or Premium/Advanced budget. Create tokens once and store them; don't create one per session.
👍
Read-only tokens for dashboards and AI agents
Giving a dashboard, tax tool or AI agent access to a user's Lighter data? Use a
read-only token
, not an API key.
Maker-only API keys
Clients on a Premium/Advanced account may mark up to 251 keys per account index as maker-only. Those keys will be restricted to 0ms speed bump transactions only:
Post-only (ALO) orders
Modify orders on ALO orders
Cancel, and Cancel All orders
The direct benefit of using this configuration is having access to an optimized execution path, with reduced scheduling latency. Keys reserved by our front-end (0-3) cannot be set as maker-only, and we apply a one-hour cooldown in between changes.
You can set a list of keys as maker-only using
setMakerOnlyApiKeys
, and get a list of maker-only keys using
getMakerOnlyApiKeys
.
How to create API keys programmatically
While generating the API keys does not require your L1 private key, associating them with your Lighter account does. See
Create accounts programmatically
for a TypeScript example, or use the
Python SDK
or the
GO SDK
. You can also interact with Lighter's smart contract directly using the
ChangePubKey function
(this is particularly helpful if you're running a multi-sig).
Nonce management
Each API key has its own nonce. Nonce rules, skipping nonces, which rejected transactions consume a nonce, and why to use a separate API key per workload are covered in
Core concepts
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.content:
Binary options markets have two outcomes. A winning share pays
1.00
USDC; a losing share pays
0
. Orders use the same transaction types and signing flow as other Lighter markets. See
Signing transactions
for client setup and transaction submission.
Up/Down
markets compare an underlying asset’s Chainlink price at the start and end of an observation window. Each window has a new market. Up wins if the closing price is at least the opening price; otherwise, Down wins.
Discover listed series and their observation windows through
events
. The asset names and durations used in these guides are examples; read each series’ configuration from the API.
Core concepts
Concept
Binary options
Market
One order book per window.
market_type
is
binary_options
, symbol
<ASSET>-UPDOWN-<DURATION>-<WINDOW START>
(window start in Unix seconds), e.g.
ETH-UPDOWN-15M-1792436400
Price
Price of one
Up
share in USDC, from
0.01
to
0.99
with a
0.01
tick (
price_decimals = 2
). It can be read as the market-implied probability of Up
Size
Number of shares. Read
size_decimals
,
min_base_amount
and
min_quote_amount
from each market returned by
events
. For example, mainnet markets checked on October 19, 2026 use four decimals, a 5-share minimum and a
0.000001
USDC quote minimum
Buy / Sell
Buying opens or adds to an
Up
position and costs
price × size
. Selling opens or adds to a
Down
position and costs
(1 − price) × size
. Trading the other side reduces your position first
Payout
settlement_cap = 100
ticks (
1.00
USDC) per winning share,
0
per losing share, paid to the USDC balance at settlement
Collateral
Every order and position is fully funded from the USDC balance. No leverage, funding or liquidation
Operator
operator_account_index
creates and settles the market. Lighter operates the Up/Down series
A
market_id
is never reused. Settled markets stay queryable, including their outcome.
📘
Use
events
to discover binary options markets. They are excluded from the unfiltered
orderBooks
listing and from
orderBookDetails

orderBookDetails
.
orderBooks?market_id=<id>

0.0000

Discover markets

Guide
Covers

Integration checklist
Discover tradable windows with
events?tag=…&active=true&sort=start_at&order=asc
. Cache each market's ID, trading window and decimals; refresh discovery as windows roll over.
If you charge partner fees, check that the client's
ApproveIntegrator

Send limit or market orders with integer prices and sizes. Up/Down markets use prices from
1
to
99

Stop submitting new orders when the trading window ends or the market leaves
active

Read positions from
bo_positions

trades
, and realized PnL from
portfolio/boPnl

Poll
events
(or subscribe to

WebSocket

Market lifecycle
status
Meaning
Orders
inactive
Listed, trading window not open yet
No orders
active
Trading window open
Create, modify, cancel
waiting-for-settlement
Window ended, outcome pending; existing GTT orders may still rest
Cancel only
in-settlement
Operator initiated settlement; remaining orders are cancelled before positions are paid
Cancel only
settled
Book drained and every position paid.
outcome
and
settlement_price
are final
–

Underlying price

not

candles

and
duration
from the selected event’s metadata. This example uses
eth
and
15m

,

eth
+
15m

1s
(the raw price observations, default) or
30s

,
end_timestamp
Unix
seconds
, inclusive, at most 24h apart
limit
1–3600, default 1000. Pass
next_cursor
as
start_timestamp
to page forward

upDownCandles

symbol
,
duration
,
resolution
,
timestamp
,
open
,
high
,
low
,
close
,
provider
and
feed_id

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.title: Partner attribution
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.content:
Partner Attribution
works on binary options with the same approval, order fields, tier requirements and reporting. This page covers the binary options parameters and fee calculation.
Client approval
Binary options are governed by the
spot
limits of the client's
ApproveIntegrator
:
max_spot_taker_fee
and
max_spot_maker_fee
. There is no binary-options-specific field. A client who has approved you with spot limits needs no new approval; a perps-only approval (spot limits
0
) must be re-sent with spot limits.
System-wide maximum
The spot maximum applies:
max_integrator_spot_taker_fee
/
max_integrator_spot_maker_fee
in
systemConfig
, currently
10000
=
1%
(perps:
1000
= 0.1%). Fee units are unchanged:
1e6
= 100%,
100
= 1 bp.
Order fields
integratorAccountIndex
,
integratorTakerFee
,
integratorMakerFee
on
CreateOrder
/
ModifyOrder
, exactly as on other markets. Non-zero fees require a Plus or Premium/Advanced client (
21520
otherwise); zero-fee attribution works on Standard.
21149
not approved / expired,
21150
above the approved maximum.
Fee calculation
The integrator fee you set is a
maximum rate
, scaled by the same price curve as the market fee and charged in USDC on the notional, to the side it applies to:
Text
integratorFee = integratorRate × size × P × (1 − P)
The client's
bo_fee_rate
discount applies to the market fee only, not to the integrator fee.
Example
With
integratorTakerFee = 5000
(a maximum rate of 0.5%), the client buys 100 Up shares at
0.51
as a taker. For the market fee, this example assumes
bo_fee_rate = 1
. Use
integratorRate = 0.005
in the formula.
Text
notional         = 100 × 0.51                    = 51.00 USDC
integrator rate  = 0.005 × (1 − 0.51)             = 0.00245 (0.245%)
integrator fee   = 51.00 × 0.00245                = 0.12495 USDC
market taker fee = 0.01 × (1 − 0.51) × 51.00     = 0.2499 USDC
The corresponding trade rates are
integrator_taker_fee: 2450
and
taker_fee: 4900
. These are rate ticks, not fee amounts in USDC. The rate stored in a trade is already scaled by the price curve. Compute the actual fee as
usd_amount × integrator_taker_fee / 1e6
(or the maker field for the maker side); do not multiply by
(1 − P)
again.
Python
Use an initialized client and a current
MARKET_ID
from
Discover markets
.
PARTNER_ACCOUNT_INDEX
is the approved fee-collecting account.
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.create_order(
    market_index=MARKET_ID,
    client_order_index=1234,
    base_amount=1000000,
    price=51,
    is_ask=False,
    order_type=client.ORDER_TYPE_LIMIT,
    time_in_force=client.ORDER_TIME_IN_FORCE_IMMEDIATE_OR_CANCEL,
    reduce_only=False,
    order_expiry=client.DEFAULT_IOC_EXPIRY,
    integrator_account_index=PARTNER_ACCOUNT_INDEX,
    integrator_taker_fee=5000,   # 0.5% max rate, ≤ client's max_spot_taker_fee
    integrator_maker_fee=0,
)
Reporting
Trades expose
integrator_taker_fee
,
integrator_taker_fee_collector_index
,
integrator_maker_fee
,
integrator_maker_fee_collector_index
(effective rate after scaling); filter with
GET /api/v1/trades?integrator_account_index=<partner>&market_type=bo
. Orders expose the requested
integrator_taker_fee
/
integrator_maker_fee
and
integrator_fee_collector_index
.
partnerStats
includes binary options volume and fees together with perps and spot. Fees are credited to the integrator account in USDC in the execution cycle after the trade.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.title: Positions and settlement
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.content:
Binary options positions are reported separately from perps positions, in
bo_positions
:
JSON
{
  "bo_positions": [
    {
      "market_id": 4206,
      "sign": 1,
      "size": "100.0000",
      "entry_quote": "51.000000",
      "avg_entry_price": "0.51"
    }
  ]
}
Field
Meaning
market_id
Binary options market ID
sign
1
holds Up;
-1
holds Down
size
Shares held, as a positive magnitude
entry_quote
Entry quote amount in USDC
avg_entry_price
Average price paid for the held side. For
sign = -1
, this is the Down price
Positions appear in
account
and in the
account_all
and
account_all_positions
WebSocket channels as
bo_positions
. The
account_market
channel reports a single market’s position as
bo_position
. See the linked sections of the
WebSocket reference
for subscription formats, authentication and response payloads.
Settlement
When the window ends the market moves to
waiting-for-settlement
. Resting GTT orders can remain until settlement; cancel them to release reserved funds sooner. When the operator initiates settlement from the price source, remaining orders are cancelled before positions are paid to the USDC balance:
Position
Settles Up (
outcome = 2
)
Settles Down (
outcome = 1
)
Up shares (
sign = 1
)
1.00
USDC per share
0
USDC
Down shares (
sign = -1
)
0
USDC
1.00
USDC per share
Market definition fields use
price ticks
. Convert them before calculating payouts in USDC:
Text
Up payout per share   = settlement_price / 10^price_decimals
Down payout per share = (settlement_cap − settlement_price) / 10^price_decimals
For Up/Down markets,
price_decimals = 2
and
settlement_cap = 100
, so
100
ticks equals
1.00
USDC.
If no outcome can be determined, the market settles at its
default_price
(
50
ticks, or
0.50
USDC per share to both sides) and
outcome
stays
0
.
Each settled position gets a
trade
with
type: "market-settlement"
, alongside regular
trade
fills. The settlement record's
price
is always in
Up terms
:
Result
price
Up wins
"1.00"
Down wins
"0.00"
Refund at the default price
"0.50"
usd_amount
is the actual USDC payout to that account. The losing side also receives a settlement record, with
usd_amount: "0.000000"
. For example, when Down wins, both sides' records have
price: "0.00"
, but only the Down holder receives a payout. The counterparty is account
281474976710655
. Settlement records carry no trading fees; handle
taker_fee
and
maker_fee
as absent or
null
. Use
usd_amount
, rather than
price × size
, to read the payout.
Realized PnL
Shell
curl -H "authorization: $AUTH" "https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/portfolio/boPnl?account_index=$ACCOUNT_INDEX"
portfolio_boPnl
(
GET /api/v1/portfolio/boPnl
, authenticated) returns realized binary options PnL grouped by event, newest first. Every outcome the account has traded is listed, including open and unsettled markets.
Parameter
Notes
account_index
Required
event_id
Return a single event
cursor
,
limit
Exclusive event id cursor (
next_cursor
),
limit
1–100
JSON
{
  "code": 200,
  "next_cursor": 106,
  "events": [
    {
      "event_id": 107,
      "event_title": "ETH Up or Down",
      "event_description": "Up if the chainlink ETH price at the end of the 15m window is at least the one at its start.",
      "total_pnl": "48.750000",
      "outcomes": [
        {
          "market_id": 4206,
          "symbol": "ETH-UPDOWN-15M-1792436400",
          "outcome": 2,
          "end_timestamp": 1792437300000,
          "settlement_pnl": "49.000000",
          "last_trade_id": 41804794,
          "total_pnl": "48.750000"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
settlement_pnl
stays
null
until the market settles with a position.
total_pnl
includes all realized PnL, including settlement,
gross of fees
: exit or settlement notional minus entry quote. Trading fees are not subtracted. To calculate net PnL, account for fees separately from the trade records. The response above is an example; IDs, prices and PnL depend on the account and event.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.title: Trading and fees
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.content:
Binary options use the same
CreateOrder
,
ModifyOrder
and
CancelOrder
transactions and the same SDK / WASM signer calls as other markets. Pass the binary options
market_id
and:
📘
For the current binary options discovery methods and response models, use
lighter-sdk 1.1.8
or newer, or
lighter-go v1.0.12
or newer. Python 1.1.8 also fixes the
boPnl
authorization header. The standard create, modify and cancel order flow is unchanged; discover binary options market IDs through
events
.
The shared-library signer uses signed 64-bit market indices (
int64
). If you call it directly from C/C++ or a custom FFI binding, use a
.h
file and bindings that match your signer library. Update declarations that still use
int cMarketIndex
to
long long int cMarketIndex
, as shown in the
current signer header
.
See the
Python binary options examples
, especially
create_order_from_event.py
, for market discovery through
events
followed by
create_order
.
Parameter
Binary options
price
Integer price ticks:
51
=
0.51
USDC. Must be
> 0
and
< settlement_cap
(
100
)
baseAmount
Integer shares × 10^
size_decimals
:
1000000
=
100.0000
shares
isAsk
0
buy = Up,
1
sell = Down
orderType
0
Limit or
1
Market only
timeInForce
0
IOC ·
1
Good-till-time ·
2
Post-only
reduceOnly
Must be
0
triggerPrice
Must be
0
(no stop / take-profit / TWAP)
Place an order
Python
Use an initialized
SignerClient
from
Signing transactions
. Set
MARKET_ID
to a current binary options market ID from
Discover markets
.
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.create_order(
    market_index=MARKET_ID,      # market_id from /api/v1/events
    client_order_index=1234,
    base_amount=1000000,         # 100.0000 shares
    price=51,                    # 0.51 USDC per Up share
    is_ask=False,                # buy = Up
    order_type=client.ORDER_TYPE_LIMIT,
    time_in_force=client.ORDER_TIME_IN_FORCE_GOOD_TILL_TIME,
    reduce_only=False,
    order_expiry=client.DEFAULT_28_DAY_ORDER_EXPIRY,
)
TypeScript (WASM)
This snippet uses the signer and submission helpers from the
TypeScript quickstart
.
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignCreateOrder(
  MARKET_ID, clientOrderIndex, 1000000, 51, 0 /* buy = Up */, 0 /* limit */, 1 /* GTT */,
  0, 0, orderExpiry,
  0, 0, 0,                    // integrator account, taker fee, maker fee
  0, 0, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
await sendTx(tx);
Order rules
Create and modify requests must pass the same trading-window, frozen-book and price-cap checks:
start_timestamp ≤ block time ≤ end_timestamp
,
is_frozen = false
, and
0 < price < settlement_cap
. A
start_timestamp
of
0
means trading can start from listing. Cancellation is allowed outside the trading window.
For resting orders, buy cost is
P × size
and sell cost is
(1 − P) × size
, where
P
is the Up price in USDC and
size
is shares. The USDC reserve is calculated
per market
as
max(Σ buy costs − Down shares held × 1.00, Σ sell costs − Up shares held × 1.00, 0)
. Buy and sell requirements are not added together; existing shares offset the opposite side. IOC and market orders are funded at fill time.
The
min_quote_amount
check uses
P × size
for both buys and sells
, even though opening a Down position costs
(1 − P) × size
. Read both minimums from
events
. For example, mainnet markets checked on October 19, 2026 have
min_base_amount = 5
shares and
min_quote_amount = 0.000001
USDC. A 5-share sell at
P = 0.02
has an Up notional of 0.10 USDC and passes that quote minimum; its Down cost is 4.90 USDC. In this configuration the 5-share base minimum is the binding minimum. Also respect
order_quote_limit
.
A market order's
price
is the worst acceptable Up price, as on other markets.
Public pool and insurance fund accounts cannot trade binary options.
Errors
Code
Message
Cause
21618
invalid order type for market
Stop, take-profit, TWAP or
reduceOnly = 1
21631
market is outside its trading window
Create or modify request before
start_timestamp
or after
end_timestamp
21632
order price must be below the full payout
Create or modify request with
price ≥ settlement_cap
21638
order book is frozen
Create or modify request while the operator has frozen the market
21752
pools are not allowed to trade in binary options markets
Public pool / insurance fund account
Orders and trades
accountActiveOrders
,
accountInactiveOrders
and
trades
accept
market_type=bo
(
all
by default) and work with a binary options
market_id
. Trades carry
market_kind: "bo"
. Settlement records use
type: "market-settlement"
; see
Positions and settlement
.
recentTrades
returns an empty list once a binary options market has settled. Use
trades
with
market_id
for historical fills and settlement records.
exchangeStats
includes binary options symbols such as
ETH-UPDOWN-…
; filter its market entries by symbol when separating market types.
Fees
Each market has a maximum
taker_fee
and
maker_fee
(Up/Down series: taker
1%
, maker
0%
). Both sides pay in USDC on the trade notional, scaled by the trade price and by the account's binary options fee multiplier:
Text
fee = marketFee × bo_fee_rate × size × P × (1 − P)
Use decimal rates in the formula:
marketFee = 0.01
for a 1% market fee.
P
is the Up price in USDC (
0.51
, not
51
price ticks).
size × P
is the Up-price notional in USDC. Opening Down costs
(1 − P) × size
; resting-order reserves follow the per-market rule above. Use the same fee formula for both sides.
(1 − P)
makes fees smaller as the outcome becomes certain: highest at
P = 0.50
, near zero at
0.01
and
0.99
.
bo_fee_rate
is the account's multiplier, the product of its binary options volume tier and LIT staking tier,
1
by default.
Binary options fees are separate from the perps/spot
account tiers
.
feeTiers
with
filter=bo
returns the
bo_tiers
(by trailing volume) and
staking_tiers
tables;
accountLimits
returns the account's
bo_user_tier_name
and
bo_fee_rate
. Read the current tables from the endpoint instead of hard-coding volume thresholds or staking discounts.
Shell
curl "https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/feeTiers?filter=bo"
Fees in trade responses
In trade JSON,
taker_fee
/
maker_fee
are the
effective rate
in fee ticks (
1e6
= 100%): with
bo_fee_rate = 1
, a 1% market taker fee on a fill at
0.51
shows as
taker_fee: 4900
(
10000 × (1 − 0.51)
), i.e.
51.00 × 0.49% = 0.2499
USDC on 100 shares.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.title: WebSocket
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/binary-.content:
Binary options markets use the shared order-book, trade and account channels listed below, alongside two binary-options-specific channels:
bo_market_stats
and
up_down_candle
. The
market_stats
and
spot_market_stats
channels exclude binary options.
Connect to
wss://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream
. Follow the existing
WebSocket reference
for connection handling and reconnects.
Shared WebSocket channels
The
WebSocket reference
covers these general-purpose channels, including their subscription formats, authentication and response payloads. For subscriptions that take a market ID, use the binary options
market_id
returned by
events
.
Channel
Binary options data
order_book/{MARKET_INDEX}
Order-book snapshots and updates for a market
trade/{MARKET_INDEX}
Public trades for a market
account_all/{ACCOUNT_ID}
Account data, with binary options positions in
bo_positions
account_all_positions/{ACCOUNT_ID}
Account positions, including
bo_positions
account_market/{MARKET_ID}/{ACCOUNT_ID}
Account data for one market, with its binary options position in
bo_position
account_orders/{MARKET_INDEX}/{ACCOUNT_ID}
and
account_all_orders/{ACCOUNT_ID}
Account orders for one market or across markets
account_all_trades/{ACCOUNT_ID}
Account trades, including binary options trades
Binary options market stats
Sends the
stats
object of a binary options market, for one market or all of them.
JSON
{
  "type": "subscribe",
  "channel": "bo_market_stats/{MARKET_INDEX}"
}
Subscribe to all binary options markets:
JSON
{
  "type": "subscribe",
  "channel": "bo_market_stats/all"
}
For
bo_market_stats/all
, the
bo_market_stats
payload is an
object keyed by market ID
, not an array. Each value is a market stats object. For a single-market subscription,
bo_market_stats
is that market's stats object directly.
The all-market stream can include old, settled and not-yet-open markets. Filter for
status: "active"
, then check
start_timestamp
,
end_timestamp
and
is_frozen
in the market definition returned by
events
before placing orders. Do not assume every market in this stream is currently tradeable.
Response fields
For a single-market update,
channel
is
bo_market_stats:{MARKET_INDEX}
,
type
is
update/bo_market_stats
, and
timestamp
is an integer. The
bo_market_stats
object contains:
Field
Type
Meaning
symbol
string
Market symbol
market_id
integer
Market ID
mid_price
,
best_ask_price
,
best_bid_price
,
last_trade_price
string
Order book and last-trade prices
daily_base_token_volume
,
daily_quote_token_volume
number
Daily base and quote volume
daily_price_low
,
daily_price_high
,
daily_price_change
number
Daily price statistics
lifetime_quote_token_volume
,
lifetime_base_token_volume
number
Lifetime quote and base volume
open_interest
string
Open interest
status
string
inactive
,
active
,
waiting-for-settlement
,
in-settlement
or
settled
outcome
integer
0
: none;
1
: No/Down;
2
: Yes/Up
See
Market lifecycle
for each status.
Up/Down candlesticks
Live candles of the underlying price of a series. Resolutions:
1s
(every price observation) and
30s
. The first message (
subscribed/up_down_candle
) is a snapshot of the last 300 candles (or fewer if less history is available); updates carry the changed candle(s).
JSON
{
  "type": "subscribe",
  "channel": "up_down_candle/{SYMBOL}/{DURATION}/{RESOLUTION}"
}
Example subscription
Use
symbol
and
duration
from the selected event’s metadata returned by
events
. The values below illustrate the channel format.
JSON
{
  "type": "subscribe",
  "channel": "up_down_candle/btc/15m/1s"
}
Response fields
For the example above,
channel
is
up_down_candle:btc:15m:1s
. Updates have
type: "update/up_down_candle"
, an integer
timestamp
, and a
candles
array. Each candle contains:
Field
Type
Meaning

string
Underlying asset, for example
btc
duration
string
Observation-window duration, for example
15m

string
1s
or
30s

integer
Candle bucket start, in Unix seconds
open
,
high
,
low
,

string
Underlying prices as decimal strings
provider
string
Price provider
feed_id
string
Underlying price feed identifier
These candles describe the underlying price feed, not the binary options order book. Use
upDownCandles
for REST history; see
Discover markets
for an example.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/choose-.title: Choose your integration
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/choose-.content:
Most integrations are one of four patterns. They differ in
who holds the keys
and
who signs transactions
.
Pattern
Who owns the Lighter account
Who signs trades
Typical product
A. Self-custodial frontend
End user (their L1 wallet)
End user's API key, generated in their browser/app
Wallets, trading UIs, super-apps
B. Server-side on behalf of users
End user
Your backend, with an API key the user approved
Copy trading, managed strategies, agents
C. Your own account
You
Your backend
Market makers, bots, funds
D. Read-only
–
Nobody (no signing)
Dashboards, analytics, portfolio trackers
A. Self-custodial frontend (most wallets and apps)
User connects their Ethereum wallet (the
L1 address
).
User deposits → Lighter creates an
account index
for them. See
Deposits, Transfers and Withdrawals
.
Your app generates an
API key pair locally
(WASM
GenerateAPIKey
), then the user signs a one-time
ChangePubKey
with their wallet to register it. See
Create accounts programmatically
.
From then on your app signs orders locally with that API key – no wallet pop-ups per trade.
Optionally, the user approves you as an
integrator
so you earn a fee on their trades. See
Partner Attribution
.
The API private key never leaves the user's device.
B. Server-side on behalf of users
Same as A, but the API key used for trading lives on your server. The user still registers the key with a one-time L1 signature. Treat these keys as highly sensitive: an API key can trade and can request
secure withdrawals
(which only go back to the user's own L1 address).
C. Your own account
Create an account by depositing, register API keys, sign and send from your backend. Consider the
Premium/Advanced

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/core-co.title: Core concepts
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/core-co.content:
L1 address
The user's
Ethereum address
. It owns the Lighter account, is used for deposits and secure withdrawals, and signs a few sensitive actions (registering an API key, transfers to other addresses, fast withdrawals, approving an integrator with fees).
Account index
Lighter's
integer ID
for an account. One L1 address can own several:
Master account
– created automatically on the first deposit.
Sub-accounts
– created with a
CreateSubAccount
transaction. Each has its own index, balances and API keys.
Public pools
– a special kind of sub-account that other users can deposit into for shares.
How indexes are assigned:
Master accounts
count
up
from 0, in order of creation. The lowest indexes (0–2) are system accounts such as the treasury and insurance fund.
Sub-accounts and pools
count
down
from
2^48 - 2
=
281474976710654
, which is the LLP. Every new sub-account, public pool or staking pool gets the next lower index.
So a small index is a master account and a very large one is a sub-account or pool. Don't assume a sub-account's index is close to its master's; look it up.
Find account indexes for an L1 address with
accountsByL1Address
. The first entry in
sub_accounts
is the master account:
Shell
curl "https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/accountsByL1Address?l1_address=0xYourAddress"
API key
An API key is a keypair (separate from the Ethereum key) that signs Lighter transactions. Each key is bound to
one account index
, uses an index from
4 to 254
(0–3 are reserved for Lighter's apps), and is registered once with an L1 signature (
ChangePubKey
). Permissions, auth tokens and maker-only keys are covered in
API keys
.
Transactions are
queued per API key
. Each key has its own nonce stream, and a transaction can't execute before the ones sent earlier on the same key.
Use separate API keys for independent workloads
Every transaction waits for a
speed bump
before it executes. The length depends on the account tier and the transaction type (for example, on Standard, taker orders wait 300 ms and post-only orders 0 ms; see
Account Types
).
Because the queue is per key, a slow transaction delays everything sent after it
on the same key
. A post-only order sent right after a taker order on the same key waits for the taker order's 300 ms.
Use a dedicated key per workload (e.g. one for quoting/cancelling, one for taking, one for transfers) so that:
delays on one workload don't hold up another, and
each workload manages its own nonces without clashing.
Premium/Advanced accounts can go further with
maker-only API keys
, which skip the speed-bump queue entirely.
Nonce
Every transaction carries a
nonce
, tracked
per API key
.
Default rule:
new_nonce = previous_nonce + 1
.
Get the next nonce:
nextNonce
(
GET /api/v1/nextNonce?account_index=…&api_key_index=…
).
Skipping nonces: set the
SkipNonce
attribute (
skip_nonce
in the Python SDK, 4th in
L2TxAttributes
) to
1
. Then any
old_nonce < new_nonce < 2^47 - 1
is accepted. Nonces are capped at
2^48 - 1
.
The Python SDK manages nonces for you. Manage them locally if you run several processes or need the lowest latency.
When a rejected transaction consumes its nonce
Where it's rejected
Examples
Nonce consumed?
API server (
sendTx
returns an error code)
Bad signature, malformed tx, wrong nonce, rate limit,
ExpiredAt
less than ~5 s away, not enough margin for a resting order
No
Sequencer, before the tx is applied
ExpiredAt
passed before execution, not enough margin or balance for a resting order (margin changed after the API accepted it), market inactive, invalid integrator fee, wrong nonce
No
Sequencer, while applying the tx
Invalid size or price, duplicate
clientOrderIndex
, wrong reduce-only direction,
orderExpiry
already passed, cancelling or modifying an unknown order
Yes
(the tx is included as a no-op)
"Resting order" means any order that can rest on the book, i.e. not IOC or TWAP.
Taker orders (IOC / market) and TWAP orders aren't margin-checked up front.
If a fill would leave the account without enough margin, the order is cancelled during matching and the nonce is consumed.
An order that executes normally and is then cancelled by matching rules (e.g. post-only would cross, IOC not filled, not enough margin for a taker fill, self-trade prevention) is a successful transaction and consumes its nonce.
When a transaction fails
without
consuming its nonce, any transactions you already sent on the same key with higher nonces will fail too. Re-sign them starting from the current
nextNonce
.
Retrying safely
Rejected by the API server:
fix the issue and resend with the
same
nonce.
Accepted (
code: 200
), outcome unknown
(timeout, dropped connection, no WebSocket confirmation):
don't
re-sign blindly. First check the tx status by hash (
GET /api/v1/tx?by=hash&value=…
) or the
account_tx
channel, and compare
nextNonce
with the nonce you used.
Executed: done, don't resend.
Failed and
nextNonce
still equals your nonce: resend with the same nonce.
Failed and the nonce was consumed: re-sign with the new
nextNonce
.
Re-signing with a
new
nonce while the original may still execute can place the order
twice
. Reusing the same
clientOrderIndex
helps: a second order with a
clientOrderIndex
that belongs to a still-open order is rejected. It doesn't protect you once the first order has filled or been cancelled, so always check status first.
Integer prices and sizes
Prices and amounts are sent as
integers
. Each market publishes its decimals via
orderBookDetails
:
JSON
{ "symbol": "ETH", "market_id": 0, "size_decimals": 4, "price_decimals": 2,
  "min_base_amount": "0.0020", "min_quote_amount": "10.000000" }
base_amount = size × 10^size_decimals
→ 0.01 ETH =
100
price = price × 10^price_decimals
→ $3,100.00 =
310000
Minimum order: the larger of
min_base_amount
(in the base asset) and
min_quote_amount
(in USDC). Minimums apply to maker orders.
For taker orders,
price
is the
worst price
you accept. If the sequencer can't fill at that price or better, the rest is cancelled.

locally (WASM / Go / Python signer) →
tx_type
,
tx_info
,
tx_hash
.
Send
via
POST /api/v1/sendTx
(or
sendTxBatch
, or WebSocket
jsonapi/sendtx
).
API response
code: 200
means
accepted
, not
executed
.
Confirm
execution via
WebSocket
account channels or
GET /api/v1/tx
.
Transaction status values are listed in
Data Structures, Constants and Errors
.
Auth tokens and account tiers
Private REST endpoints and WebSocket channels need an
auth token
signed by an API key, or a
read-only token
. See
API keys
.
Fees, latency and limits depend on the account tier (
Standard
,
Plus
,
Premium/Advanced
). See
Account Types
and
Rate Limits
.

Deposit via Ethereum Mainnet
To deposit via Ethereum mainnet, you can use the
deposit
method (0x8a857083) directly. You'll need to specify  the following parameters:
deposit
: the amount of Ether you're depositing. That is optional and only needed when interacting with the contract directly, Lighter's Ethereum gateway page does not require this. You can leave this at zero if you're depositing other kinds of assets.
_to
: the L1 address you want to credit the deposit to
_assetIndex
: the asset you want to deposit. You can grab the correct asset id from the
assetDetails
endpoint
_routeType
: whether you want to deposit the asset to your perps (0), or spot account (1). Only USDC can be deposited to your perps account
_amount
: the amount you're depositing.
it should be in line with the ERC20's decimals. E.g. 6 decimals for USDC, 18 decimals for Ether etc. 1 USDC, or equivalent, minimum.
If you're depositing assets different from ETH (e.g. USDC), make sure to approve spending for Lighter's smart contract (0x3B4D794a66304F130a4Db8F2551B0070dfCf5ca7) for that ERC20. There is a minimum of 1 USDC, and equivalent for other ERC20s, per deposit.
Example with
viem
, where
wallet
is a WalletClient connected to the user's wallet on Ethereum mainnet:
TypeScript
import { parseUnits, erc20Abi } from "viem";

const LIGHTER = "0x3B4D794a66304F130a4Db8F2551B0070dfCf5ca7";
const USDC = "0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48";
const amount = parseUnits("100", 6);

await wallet.writeContract({ address: USDC, abi: erc20Abi, functionName: "approve", args: [LIGHTER, amount] });
await wallet.writeContract({
  address: LIGHTER,
  abi: lighterAbi, // fetch from Etherscan (proxy implementation)
  functionName: "deposit",
  args: [userAddress, usdcAssetIndex, 0 /* perps */, amount],
});

https://bridge.lighter.xyz
Authentication
: every request needs to include
x-api-key
in its header. Builders can contact us through
Discord tickets
via #support to request one.
For new users, depositing will automatically create an account on Lighter and assign the wallet an
account_index
.

Create a Universal Deposit Address (UDA)
POST
request to
https://bridge.lighter.xyz/v1/uda
Content-Type
:
application/json
Field
Type
Notes
walletAddress
string
The client's EVM wallet, where funds will be credited
market
string
"perps"
or
"spot"
asset
string
"USDC"
or
"ETH"
. This is what the deposit asset gets converted to, when credited on Lighter
accountIndex
number
Optional. It can be used to target a sub-account; if you omit it, the deposit is credited to the master account index.
JSON Body example
JSON
{
  "walletAddress": "0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111",
  "market": "perps",
  "asset": "USDC"
}
Example Response (200)
JSON
{
  "depositAddr": "0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222",
  "solanaAddr": "So1anaDepositAddressExample11111111111111111",
  "tronAddr": "TTronDepositAddressExample1234567890",
  "btcAddrSegwit": "bc1qexampledepositaddress0000000000000000",
  "blocked": false,
  "resolved": {
    "toChainId": "3586256", // lighter's chain id
    "toTokenAddress": "0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48",
    "actionType": "LIGHTER_PERPS",
    "recipientAddr": "1234", // client's account index, or l1 if the account is new
    "userId": "0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111"
  }
}
Deposit addresses are used to route and credit the amount to the client's address (returned as
userId
and
recipientAddr
). Show the address for the chain the user picks, and check
blocked
before displaying it. Call the bridge API
server-side only
: never expose the
x-api-key
in a client.

Track Deposit Status
GET
request to
https://bridge.lighter.xyz/v1/uda/status/{walletAddress}
walletAddress
is the client's wallet, the same one used to generate a UDA above, and returned as
userId
.
Example Response (200)
JSON
{
  "transactions": [
    {
      "fromChainId": "42161",
      "fromTokenAddress": "0xaf88d065e77c8cC2239327C5EDb3A432268e5831",
      "fromAmountBaseUnit": "4999999",
      "toChainId": "3586256",
      "toTokenAddress": "0xA0b86991c6218b36c1d19D4a2e9Eb0cE3606eB48",
      "txHash": "0xabc123...",
      "createdTimeMs": 1787068237169,
      "status": "COMPLETED",
      "depositAddr": "0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222"
    }
  ]
}
Deposits appear with status:
"PROCESSING"
shortly after the user’s transaction confirms on the source chain, and moves to
"COMPLETED"
once the funds are credited on Lighter, typically within a few minutes.
Errors
Example error
JSON
{ "errorCode": "InvalidParameterError", "errorMsg": "market must be \"spot\" or \"perps\"" }
HTTP
errorCode
Meaning
400
InvalidParameterError
Malformed body, unsupported market/asset, bad address
403
InsufficientPermissionError
Missing/invalid API key, or wallet not generated by you
502
DependencyFailureError
Upstream temporarily unavailable, retry with backoff
Example (TypeScript)
TypeScript
const BASE = "https://bridge.lighter.xyz";
const KEY = process.env.LIGHTER_BUILDER_KEY!; // server-side only

async function createDepositAddress(walletAddress: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/v1/uda`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-api-key": KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ walletAddress, market: "perps", asset: "USDC" }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`UDA mint failed: ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json();
}

async function getDepositQuote(body: {
  fromAmountBaseUnit: string;
  fromChainId: string;
  fromTokenAddress: string;
  recipientAddress: string;
  toChainId: string;
  toTokenAddress: string;
}) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/v1/uda/quote`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-api-key": KEY, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`quote failed: ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json();
}

async function getDepositStatus(walletAddress: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/v1/uda/status/${walletAddress}`, {
    headers: { "x-api-key": KEY },
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`status failed: ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json();
}
[Legacy] Deposit USDC via other EVM-compatible chains
The following chains are supported via Circle's CCTP: Arbitrum, Base, Avalanche C-Chain, Arc. Minimum deposit is 5 USDC. You can either generate an intent address via the front-end, or via
API
:
Shell
curl -X POST https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/createIntentAddress \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "chain_id=42161&from_addr=0xyourL1address&amount=0&is_external_deposit=true"
Available networks can be fetched, together with their Chain ID, via the
deposit/networks
endpoint.
Withdrawals: Secure and Fast
You can process both
secure
,
fast withdrawals
, and
transfers
via both SDKs, you can find linked examples with the Python SDK. The TypeScript examples below use the WASM signer and
sendTx
helper from
Signing Transactions
.

Withdrawals and transfers have their own per-transaction-type limits; see
Rate Limits
.
Secure withdrawal
Funds can only go to the L1 address that owns the account, so the API key alone is enough.
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignWithdraw(
  assetIndex,   // from /api/v1/assetDetails
  0,            // routeType: 0 = perps, 1 = spot
  amount,       // integer in the asset's Lighter decimals (USDC: 6)
  0, await nextNonce(), API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
await sendTx(tx);
The withdrawal is finalized on Ethereum. Lighter usually claims it for the user; if not, the user can call
withdrawPendingBalance
on the contract (see
Priority Transactions
). If you prefer, you can also process secure withdrawals from the contract directly, using the
withdraw
(0xd20191bd) method.
Transfer between Lighter accounts
Use transfers to move funds between a user's master and sub-accounts, or to another user.
Get the fee:
transferFeeInfo
(
GET /api/v1/transferFeeInfo?account_index=…&to_account_index=…
, authenticated). The fee is charged
on top
of the amount and must match exactly.
Sign:
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignTransfer(
  toAccountIndex,
  assetIndex,
  0,               // fromRouteType: 0 perps, 1 spot
  0,               // toRouteType
  amount,          // integer, asset decimals
  fee.transfer_fee_usdc,
  "0x" + "00".repeat(32), // memo: 32 bytes
  0, await nextNonce(), API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
If the destination belongs to a
different owner
(a different master account), have the owner's wallet sign
tx.messageToSign
and set
txInfo.L1Sig
(same pattern as
ChangePubKey
). Transfers between the same owner's accounts need no wallet signature, even though
messageToSign
is still returned. See
When an L1 signature is required
.
Send with
sendTx
.
Fast withdrawal (USDC)
A fast withdrawal is a transfer to Lighter's fast-withdraw pool with the destination address encoded in the memo:
fastwithdraw/info
(
GET /api/v1/fastwithdraw/info?account_index=…
, authenticated) →
to_account_index
,
withdraw_limit
.
transferFeeInfo
for that
to_account_index
.
Build
memo
= destination address (20 bytes) + 12 zero bytes.
SignTransfer(...)
to the pool account, collect the
L1 signature
.
fastwithdraw
(
POST /api/v1/fastwithdraw
) with form fields
tx_info
and
to_address
.
Reference implementation:
withdraw_fast.py
.

,

and
transfer_history
return past movements. See

They are all initialized as empty with zero bids and asks. Since there are no market makers, expect liquidity to be low (or zero). To test order fills, you may need to provide liquidity yourself by placing resting orders from one account and submitting matching orders from another.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-cor.title: Signing Core transactions
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-cor.content:
Applications can construct and sign transactions locally, then submit them directly to Core. Depending on the operation, authorization requires an API-key signature, the account controller's signature, or both. See
Accounts
for the authorization model.
Lighter's
TypeScript and WASM quickstart
explains the JavaScript setup and signing workflow. Its
transaction guides
and
WASM signer reference
cover the existing transaction types. This page follows the same workflow for the additional transaction types available on the devnet.
Set up the signer
Follow Lighter's
TypeScript and WASM quickstart
, but use the
evm-devnet
branch of
lighter-go
. It retains the existing signing methods and adds WASM exports for
SignSendToEvm
and
SignWithdrawToL1Address
.
Replace the quickstart's clone command with the following.
Bash
git clone --branch evm-devnet \
  https://github.com/elliottech/lighter-go.git lighter-go
cd lighter-go
Build the
./wasm/
target described in the quickstart and use the resulting
lighter-signer.wasm
, with
wasm_exec.js
from the same Go version. The new methods are not in upstream release binaries or the devnet preview version's
web-wasm
target.
The examples below use the quickstart's reusable
signer.ts
module
with the devnet preview WASM binary built above. The module exports
lighter
and
check
.
check
throws when a signer call returns an error. The
browser setup
uses the same signing methods.
Generate an API-key pair
With the signer set up, call
GenerateAPIKey()
to generate a key pair locally.
TypeScript
import { lighter, check } from "./signer";

const { privateKey, publicKey } = check(lighter.GenerateAPIKey());
Generating the pair does not require a wallet signature or submit a transaction. Before using the key to sign routine Core transactions,
register it on the Core account
.
Initialize the signing client
Set
LIGHTER_URL
to your network's Core API URL and
LIGHTER_CHAIN_ID
to its
Core chain ID
, not its EVM or L1 chain ID. The devnet Core chain ID is
300
; see
Chain Info
. Do not keep the upstream quickstart's mainnet defaults.
Use the account index, API-key index, and API private key for a key already registered on that Core account.
TypeScript
import { lighter, check } from "./signer";

const CORE_API_URL = process.env.LIGHTER_URL!;
const CORE_CHAIN_ID = Number(process.env.LIGHTER_CHAIN_ID);
const ACCOUNT_INDEX = Number(process.env.LIGHTER_ACCOUNT_INDEX);
const API_KEY_INDEX = Number(process.env.LIGHTER_API_KEY_INDEX);
const API_PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.LIGHTER_API_PRIVATE_KEY!;

check(lighter.CreateClient(
  "", API_PRIVATE_KEY, CORE_CHAIN_ID, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));

async function nextNonce(): Promise<number> {
  const res = await fetch(
    `${CORE_API_URL}/api/v1/nextNonce?account_index=${ACCOUNT_INDEX}&api_key_index=${API_KEY_INDEX}`,
  ).then(r => r.json());
  if (res.code !== 200) throw new Error(res.message);
  return res.nonce;
}
Keep HTTP requests in JavaScript and pass an explicit nonce to the signer. Use one Core chain ID per WASM instance. The bindings take JavaScript numbers for integer arguments, so keep them within
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
.
Core-assigned spot
orderIndex
values exceed this limit because they encode the market index above the low 48 bits. When placing a spot order, set a unique, nonzero
clientOrderIndex
for the account, then pass it as the order index to
SignCancelOrder(...)
or
SignModifyOrder(...)
. Client order indexes are at most
2^48 - 1
, so they fit safely in a JavaScript number.
Sign the devnet transaction types
Choose one of the following calls. Each returns
txType
,
txInfo
,
txHash
, and
messageToSign
.
txInfo
is a JSON string containing the API-key signature. Signing does not submit the transaction.
Send to EVM
This example signs a transfer of
0.01
ETH from the account's spot balance. Set
EVM_RECIPIENT
to the recipient and
LIGHTER_SEND_TO_EVM_FEE
to the fee required by your network, in
Core USDC base units
. See
Send to EVM
for balance, fee, and authorization requirements.
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignSendToEvm(
  1,                                           // assetIndex: ETH
  process.env.EVM_RECIPIENT!,                  // evmRecipient
  1,                                           // routeType: spot
  1_000_000,                                   // baseAmount: 0.01 ETH
  Number(process.env.LIGHTER_SEND_TO_EVM_FEE), // usdcFee
  await nextNonce(),
  API_KEY_INDEX,
  ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
Withdraw to L1 Address
This example signs a withdrawal of
0.01
ETH from the account's spot balance. Set
L1_RECIPIENT
to the recipient on L1. See
Core to L1
for withdrawal requirements and finalization.
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignWithdrawToL1Address(
  1,                         // assetIndex: ETH
  process.env.L1_RECIPIENT!, // l1Recipient
  1,                         // routeType: spot
  1_000_000,                 // baseAmount: 0.01 ETH
  await nextNonce(),
  API_KEY_INDEX,
  ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
Add controller authorization
The WASM signer returns
messageToSign
, which the account controller signs using EIP-191 personal-sign. The application then attaches the signature before submission. For these two new transaction types, the signature field is
OwnerSig
rather than
L1Sig
.
Withdraw to L1 Address always requires the EOA controller's signature. Send to EVM requires it unless the recipient's EVM-controlled Core account index is exactly the account being debited. Sending from a subaccount to its master's EVM address still requires the signature.
When the signature is required, collect and attach it as follows. Here,
walletClient
is a connected viem wallet client and
controllerAddress
is the Core master account's controlling EOA. Sign
messageToSign
, not
txHash
.
TypeScript
const ownerSig = await walletClient.signMessage({
  account: controllerAddress,
  message: tx.messageToSign,
});

tx.txInfo = JSON.stringify({
  ...JSON.parse(tx.txInfo),
  OwnerSig: ownerSig,
});
For a Send to EVM transfer that does not require controller authorization, leave
txInfo
unchanged. A contract controller must use its
native-domain method
when controller authorization is required.
Submit to Core
Submit the signed JSON to the network's Core API using
sendTx
.
TypeScript
const res = await fetch(`${CORE_API_URL}/api/v1/sendTx`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    tx_type: String(tx.txType),
    tx_info: tx.txInfo,
  }),
}).then(r => r.json());

if (res.code !== 200) throw new Error(`sendTx ${res.code}: ${res.message}`);
API acceptance does not confirm successful execution on Core. Use Lighter's
transaction lookup
to check the Core outcome. A transaction with
status
of
2
(executed) or
3
(packed) may still have failed during Core execution. Parse the JSON string in
event_info
and check its
ae
field, which is empty on success or contains a JSON-encoded error on failure. A transaction that fails this way still consumes its nonce, so fetch the next nonce before signing a retry.
For the new transaction types covered on this page, successful execution on Core is followed by delivery or finalization on the destination domain. Follow the corresponding guide after confirming success on Core.
Send to EVM.
See
EVM delivery
.
Withdraw to L1 Address.
See
L1 withdrawal finalization
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-dif.title: Differences from L1 EVM
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-dif.content:
Lighter EVM mirrors Ethereum L1 EVM semantics as of the Fusaka BPO2 fork, with the following deviations.
Chain metadata
The Chain ID is
chainId = 19_529 = 0x4C49 = "LI"
The block time is 1 second.
Transaction model differences
Blob txs are not supported:
EIP-4844
blob transaction type
0x03
is unsupported.
New exogenous transaction type:
Lighter EVM introduces one new
EIP-2718
transaction type (
0x7E
) for handling deposits from L1 (and other non-user-originated protocol flows such as Core -> EVM async writes and protocol upgrades).
EIP-1559 parameters differ from Ethereum mainnet defaults:
EIP-1559
parameters are used.
TARGET_GAS_LIMIT = 4,250,000
ELASTICITY_MULTIPLIER = 4
(
MAX_GAS_LIMIT = 17,000,000
)
BASE_FEE_MAX_CHANGE_DENOMINATOR = 334
INITIAL_BASE_FEE = 1 gwei
Priority transactions (L1-originated transactions) fee parameters:
MAX_PRIORITY_GAS_LIMIT = 10,000,000
BASE_FEE_OVERHEAD = 120,000
BASE_FEE_SCALAR = 9,700,000,000,000
Base fee burn
Unlike L1 Ethereum, Lighter EVM sends base fees to the
BaseFeeVault
instead of burning them.
L1 data fee
In addition to the ordinary execution fee, every fee-paying transaction pays for its metered L1 data contribution. The fee is exposed on receipts through
l1Fee
,
l1GasUsed
, and
l1GasPrice
; see
L1 Data Fee
.
Support for L1 predeploys
EIP-2935
contract (
0x0000F90827F1C53a10cb7A02335B175320002935
) serves the most recent
8191
Lighter EVM
block hashes (not Ethereum L1 block hashes).
EIP-4788
contract (
0x000F3df6D732807Ef1319fB7B8bB8522d0Beac02
) is not supported (no code).
EIP-7002
contract (
0x00000961Ef480Eb55e80D19ad83579A64c007002
) is not supported (no code).
EIP-7251
contract (
0x0000BBdDc7CE488642fb579F8B00f3a590007251
) is not supported (no code).
There are additional new predeploys specific to Lighter EVM; see
Chain info
.
Opcodes and precompiles
PREVRANDAO
:
always returns
0
.
COINBASE
:
always returns
SEQUENCER_FEE_VAULT_ADDR
.
BLOBHASH
/
BLOBBASEFEE
:
are treated as invalid opcodes and result in exceptional halt.
READ_CORE_ADDR
precompile (
0x6600000000000000000000000000000000000000
):
precompile for reading Core state. Returns (
bytes memory data
), where
data
is arbitrary data from the Core read.
See
Reading Core from EVM
for more details on how
READ_CORE_ADDR
is used.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-get.title: Getting Started
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-get.content:
This guide shows how to send your first transaction on Lighter EVM using
cast
.
Before you start:
use a disposable account that you control
obtain access to the Lighter EVM RPC endpoint
fund your account with Lighter EVM ETH
Prerequisites
Install Foundry (if not already installed), then make sure
cast
is available:
Bash
cast --version
1. Export environment variables
Bash
export LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL="<lighter_evm_rpc_url>"
export LIGHTER_EVM_PRIVATE_KEY="<your_private_key>"
export RECIPIENT="0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111"
2. Confirm your setup
Check the chain ID:
Bash
cast chain-id --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"
This should return Lighter EVM chain ID
chainId = 19_529 = 0x4C49 = "LI"
.
Get your sender address from the private key:
Bash
export SENDER="$(cast wallet address --private-key "$LIGHTER_EVM_PRIVATE_KEY")"
echo "$SENDER"
Check sender balance:
Bash
cast balance "$SENDER" --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"
3. Send a transaction with
cast
Send a simple ETH transfer:
Bash
# Lighter EVM also derives its data-availability pubdata budget from the gas limit,
# so a plain transfer needs more than Ethereum's standard 21,000 gas.
cast send "$RECIPIENT" \
  --value 0.001ether \
  --gas-limit 30000 \
  --private-key "$LIGHTER_EVM_PRIVATE_KEY" \
  --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"
cast send
prints the transaction hash and receipt fields after submission.
4. Verify the transaction
Inspect the transaction:
Bash
cast tx <TX_HASH> --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"
Inspect the receipt:
Bash
cast receipt <TX_HASH> --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"
Check recipient balance:
Bash
cast balance "$RECIPIENT" --rpc-url "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL"

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.title: Lighter Interop
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
The Lighter protocol spans Ethereum L1, Lighter EVM, and Lighter Core. It natively enables interoperability between these three domains so that applications can act across domains and assets can move between supported representations.
The following sections introduce the concepts and interfaces for working across these domains.
Accounts
explains account types and authorization across the three domains.
Reading Core from EVM
describes how EVM contracts access Core state synchronously.
Message passing
outlines the interfaces for sending messages across domains.
Tokens
provides an overview of how the protocol builds on the messaging infrastructure described above to represent and move value across domains.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.title: Accounts
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
Lighter EVM and Lighter Core use separate account models. This page explains both models and how an EVM address can control a Core account.
Lighter EVM accounts
Lighter EVM uses the same account model and address format as Ethereum L1: accounts are either externally owned accounts (EOAs) or smart contracts, identified by a 20-byte address. Account state is independent between L1 and Lighter EVM.
Core accounts
Core has master accounts and subaccounts. Each subaccount belongs to, and is controlled by, exactly one master account. Every Core account maintains its own state, including balances, orders, positions, and API keys.
Every Core account is uniquely identified by a
uint48 accountIndex
assigned when the account is created. Master account indices are in
[0, 2^47 - 1]
, while subaccount indices are in
[2^47, 2^48 - 2]
.
A master account is created when the protocol processes the first deposit for a previously unregistered address. Once the master account exists, subaccounts can be created under it.
Master accounts are also well-indexed by the tuple
(domain, address)
, where
domain
is either Ethereum L1 or Lighter EVM. Each tuple identifies at most one Core master account, and each master account has exactly one controlling tuple. Core therefore treats the same 20-byte address on Ethereum L1 and Lighter EVM as two distinct controllers.
EVM-controlled accounts
An EVM-controlled master account is indexed by
(Lighter EVM, address)
, where
address
may identify an EOA or a smart contract.
Core creates the master account when it processes the first
deposit from Lighter EVM
to the controlling EVM address.
Once the account is created, you can retrieve its
accountIndex
from Lighter EVM using the
EVM account index
read.
The controlling address operates the master account and its subaccounts through the
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
and
EvmInteropManager
predeploys; see
EVM and Core
.
L1-controlled accounts
An L1-controlled master account is indexed by
(Ethereum L1, address)
.
Core creates the master account when it processes the first deposit from Ethereum L1 to the controlling L1 address. The controlling address operates the master account and its subaccounts from L1 and cannot operate them from Lighter EVM.
These accounts can only be created by deposits from L1.
Account authorization
Core recognizes two forms of authorization:
API-key authorization
and
master authorization
.
API-key authorization
An API key authorizes its holder to submit routine Core transactions, such as placing and cancelling orders, without obtaining separate approval from the master account’s controller for each transaction.
The key holder signs these transactions and submits them directly to Core, without sending an Ethereum L1 or Lighter EVM transaction. The controller may hold the API key itself or allow a separate operator to hold it. For example, a smart contract can register a key held by an off-chain operator, allowing that operator to trade on the contract’s behalf.
Accounts created through deposits initially have no API keys. The master account’s controller must authorize registering the first key and can later update or revoke it.
For what an API key can do, including on subaccounts, see Lighter's
API keys guide
.
GET /api/v1/accountsByEvmAddress?evm_address=...
lists an EVM-controlled account's subaccounts.
To generate an API-key pair locally, see
generate an API-key pair
in the Signing Core transactions guide.
An API key can be registered in three ways.
From Core.
An EOA controller of an L1-controlled or EVM-controlled account can submit a signed
ChangePubKey
transaction (
txType = 8
). It requires a signature from the new API key and the controller's ECDSA signature, so no previously registered key is needed. See
Lighter's API-key registration guide
.
From EVM.
The controller of an EVM-controlled account calls
EvmToCoreEntrypoint.changePubKey(...)
.
From L1.
The controller of an L1-controlled account calls
L1CoreMessaging.changePubKey(...)
.
See
Signing Core transactions
for setting up the WASM signer and submitting transactions directly to Core.
Master authorization
Master authorization is explicit approval from the master account’s controller. It is required to manage API keys and to perform certain sensitive operations, such as withdrawals to L1. A directly submitted Core transaction may require API-key authorization, master authorization, or both, depending on the operation.
The controller can provide master authorization in either of two ways:
By signature.
If the controlling address is an EOA, it can provide an ECDSA signature
authorizing the operation
.
From its controlling domain.
The controller can call the corresponding method on Ethereum L1 or Lighter EVM. The authenticated caller provides master authorization, so a separate ECDSA signature is unnecessary.
A smart contract cannot produce an ECDSA signature. A contract-controlled account must therefore use the appropriate L1-initiated or EVM-initiated method when master authorization is required. It can still register an API key that an off-chain operator uses for routine transactions requiring only API-key authorization.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.title: Message passing
EVM and Core
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
EVM and Core communicate through stateful write streams, one in each direction. These streams are
settled on L1
together with Core and EVM state, allowing the sequencer to fulfill cross-domain write requests without waiting for L1 finality.
Rather than exposing arbitrary cross-domain messaging, the protocol defines a fixed set of operations that users can request on each domain.
Writes are
asynchronous
and processed first-in, first-out within each direction. The sequencer aims to fulfill requests as soon as possible, but the protocol does not guarantee a fixed delay between submission on one domain and fulfillment on the other.
Pending writes have the same censorship-resistance protection as L1 priority requests. If a write remains unfulfilled past its 14-day expiration period, the
escape hatch
can be activated on L1.
EVM to Core
EVM accounts can request actions on Core, such as placing orders or transferring tokens. Each request is submitted on EVM and processed asynchronously by Core.
Two EVM
predeploys
provide access to these writes.
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
defines the supported writes. Most methods can be called directly by users. Some token-related methods can only be called by
EvmInteropManager
.
EvmInteropManager
handles token-specific logic before calling the restricted entrypoint methods. See
Token transfers
and
Token linking
for those flows.
Every write ultimately passes through
EvmToCoreMessenger
, which emits the request as raw bytes for Core to consume. However, its submission method accepts calls only from
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
, so users cannot bypass the supported operations to send arbitrary messages to Core.
Submitting a write to Core
Submit a write to Core through one of the two predeploys introduced above. Every submitted write is assigned a
uint64 reqId
that identifies the request on Core. The write methods return this ID.
If the EVM call reverts, no request is submitted. A successful EVM transaction confirms only that the request was submitted, not that Core executed it.
The Core sequencer validates each request against the state immediately before execution. This state may differ from what an earlier EVM read returned.
Core fulfillment can fail for various reasons, documented under each
supported write
. Since submission and fulfillment are not atomic, a failure on Core does not revert the initiating EVM transaction.
A failed request is still consumed and cannot be replayed. Trying again requires submitting a new request with a new
reqId
.
Multiple writes submitted in one EVM transaction are processed independently on Core, not atomically. One can succeed while another fails.
Keep the
reqId
to track the request's status and read its outcome from Core, as described in
Reading the result of a write
.
Reading the result of a write
Core records a status and a response for every request it processes. To retrieve them, call
READ_CORE
with the
transaction-status selector
(
0x0000
) and the request's
reqId
:
Solidity
(bool success, bytes memory result) = READ_CORE.staticcall(
    abi.encodePacked(uint16(0x0000), reqId)
);
(uint8 status, bytes memory data) = abi.decode(result, (uint8, bytes));
Interpret the returned
status
and
data
using the following table.
status
Meaning
data
0
Core has not processed the request yet.
Empty.
1
Core executed the write successfully.
The write's return value, or empty if it has none.
2
Core executed the write, but it failed with an error.
abi.encode(uint32(errorCode))
.
Each operation's
Core response
section describes its success data (
status == 1
) and possible error codes (
status == 2
).
When the result is visible.
The result is never available in the EVM transaction that submitted the write. It appears in a later EVM block, once Core processes the request. Check from a later transaction, or poll off-chain with
eth_call
, until
status
is nonzero.
Pending versus unknown.
Status
0
is also returned for request IDs that have never been issued.
EvmToCoreMessenger.reqId()
returns the next request ID to be assigned. A request is pending if its status is
0
and its
reqId
is less than this counter.
Example: submit, then read the result
The following contract submits a cancel-all request and exposes its outcome. The contract is the sender of the write, so it must control an
EVM-controlled Core master account
, and
accountIndex
must identify that master account or one of its subaccounts.
🚧
Warning
Core treats the immediate EVM caller as the authority for a write. For a contract-controlled Core account, this is the contract that calls
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
. Such contracts should enforce any desired access control over who may trigger Core writes through them.
Solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

interface IEvmToCoreEntrypoint {
    function cancelAllOrders(uint48 accountIndex) external returns (uint64 reqId);
}

contract CoreWriter {
    address constant READ_CORE = 0x6600000000000000000000000000000000000000;
    IEvmToCoreEntrypoint constant ENTRYPOINT =
        IEvmToCoreEntrypoint(0x6600000000000000000000000000000000000009);

    address public immutable owner;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    // Step 1: submit the request. Core executes it in a later Core block.
    function cancelAll(uint48 accountIndex) external returns (uint64 reqId) {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "not owner");
        reqId = ENTRYPOINT.cancelAllOrders(accountIndex);
    }

    // Step 2: read the outcome from a later EVM block or with eth_call.
    function cancelAllResult(uint64 reqId)
        external
        view
        returns (uint8 status, uint64 ordersToCancel, uint32 errorCode)
    {
        (bool success, bytes memory result) = READ_CORE.staticcall(
            abi.encodePacked(uint16(0x0000), reqId)
        );
        require(success, "Core status read failed");

        bytes memory data;
        (status, data) = abi.decode(result, (uint8, bytes));
        if (status == 1) {
            ordersToCancel = abi.decode(data, (uint64));
        } else if (status == 2) {
            errorCode = abi.decode(data, (uint32));
        }
    }
}
Core transaction hash
Core APIs identify a fulfilled write by its Core transaction hash. To derive it, decode the
WriteToCore(address indexed sender, uint64 indexed reqId, bytes writeRequest)
event emitted by
EvmToCoreMessenger
in the EVM transaction receipt. Use the event's
sender
,
reqId
, and full
writeRequest
, including its transaction-type byte.
The following helper uses the network's
Core chain ID
, not its EVM chain ID. It hashes the packed fields, appends eight zero bytes, and returns the 80-character hexadecimal string expected by Core APIs, without a
0x
prefix.
ts
import { encodePacked, keccak256, padHex, type Address, type Hex } from 'viem';

function coreTxHash(
  coreChainId: number,
  sender: Address,
  reqId: bigint,
  writeRequest: Hex,
): string {
  const digest = keccak256(encodePacked(
    ['string', 'uint32', 'uint64', 'address', 'bytes'],
    ['zkl/toCoreTx/v1', coreChainId, reqId, sender, writeRequest],
  ));
  return padHex(digest, { size: 40, dir: 'right' }).slice(2);
}
If an EVM transaction submits multiple writes, select the event for the intended
reqId
. Each write has its own Core transaction hash. Use this hash when
retrieving a Core-originated L1 Call
.
Supported writes
The following methods belong to
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
.
Function
Description
changePubKey
Update or revoke a Core API key.
createOrder
Place an order on a Core market.
cancelOrder
Cancel an order by its Core or client identifier.
cancelAllOrders
Cancel all open orders for a Core account.
registerSendToCore
Request a deposit credit on Core. Callable only by
EvmInteropManager
.
finalizeEvmLink
Notify Core of an EVM-native asset's canonical token. Callable only by
EvmInteropManager
.
registerSendToEvm
Request a Core balance debit and delivery on EVM. Callable only by
EvmInteropManager
.
burnShares
Burn public-pool shares held by a Core account.
withdrawToL1Address
Request a withdrawal from a Core balance to an L1 recipient.
Each
Core response
describes the
status
and
data
returned when
reading the result of a write
.
Change public key
Call
EvmToCoreEntrypoint.changePubKey
to update or revoke a Core API key. The
apiKeyIndex
identifies the key to update, and
pubKey
supplies its new public key.
The sender must control an
EVM-controlled Core master account
, and
accountIndex
must identify that master account, one of its subaccounts, or a public pool it controls. Staking pool accounts are not supported.
Call
Solidity
function changePubKey(
    uint48 accountIndex,
    uint8 apiKeyIndex,
    bytes calldata pubKey
) external returns (uint64 reqId);
Parameters
Type
Parameter
Description
uint48
accountIndex
Core account whose API key is updated.
uint8
apiKeyIndex
Index of the API key to update, from
0
to
254
.
bytes
pubKey
