https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
The L1 bridge
ZkLighter
intermediates messaging between L1 and Core.
Arbitrary cross-domain messaging is not supported. The protocol defines a fixed set of messages that can be sent between L1 and Core.
L1 to Core
L1 accounts can request actions on Core, such as placing orders or transferring tokens. Each request is submitted to a priority queue on L1 and processed asynchronously by the Core sequencer in first-in, first-out order.
Two L1 contracts provide access to these requests.
L1CoreMessaging
exposes all supported L1-to-Core writes. Some methods are restricted to
L1InteropManager
or governance.
L1InteropManager
handles token-specific logic and permissions before calling the restricted
L1CoreMessaging
methods. See
Token transfers
and
Token linking
for those flows.
Every request ultimately passes through
ZkLighter.addPriorityRequestExt(...)
. This is the bridge's general mechanism for adding Core priority requests, but it accepts calls only from
L1CoreMessaging
. Thus, users can only submit supported operations to Core rather than engaging in arbitrary messaging.
L1-controlled Core accounts can use this priority queue to bypass censorship of transactions submitted directly to Core. The Core sequencer is obligated to process these requests. If the oldest pending request remains unfulfilled past its 14-day expiration, anyone can activate the
escape hatch
, allowing L1-controlled accounts to exit their balances on L1.
For EVM-controlled Core accounts, circumvention of sequencer downtime or censorship is covered in
L1 and EVM message passing
.
Submitting a priority request to Core
Submit a request to Core through the appropriate L1 contract introduced above. To authorize operations on an existing account,
L1CoreMessaging
resolves the caller's L1-controlled master account and includes its index in the request. The same address on Lighter EVM does not authorize an L1-controlled account, or vice versa. See
Accounts
.
If the L1 call reverts, no request is submitted. A successful L1 transaction confirms only submission, not successful execution on Core. Since submission and fulfillment are not atomic, a failure on Core does not revert the initiating L1 transaction.
GET /api/v1/txFromL1TxHash?hash=...
returns the Core transaction for an L1 transaction hash. Core includes every priority request, so
status
is
3
once Core has processed the request, whether or not the operation succeeded. The outcome is the
ae
field of
event_info
: both are JSON strings, and
ae
is empty on success. On failure it holds a
Core error code
:
JSON
{
  "status": 3,
  "event_info": "{\"a\":4,\"f\":0,\"ti\":0,\"ae\":\"{\\\"code\\\":21128,\\\"message\\\":\\\"invalid master account index\\\"}\"}"
}
L1CoreMessaging
does not check that the caller controls the target
accountIndex
; Core does. The request above targeted an account under another master account, so L1 accepted it and Core rejected it with
21128
.
If Core processing produces an outgoing message, track that delivery separately. For example,
L1CoreMessaging.sendToEvm(...)
requests a debit on Core, which then schedules a transfer to EVM. See
L1-initiated send to EVM
for the full flow.
Supported requests
Users can directly call the following methods on
L1CoreMessaging
to submit account operations.
Method
Requested Core operation
changePubKey(...)
Register or replace an API key.
createOrder(...)
Reduce or close a perps position: Core runs it as a reduce-only, immediate-or-cancel order.
cancelAllOrders(...)
Cancel the account's orders.
burnShares(...)
Redeem public-pool shares.
withdraw(...)
Initiate a
withdrawal to L1
.
withdrawToL1Address(...)
Initiate a
withdrawal to a specified L1 recipient
.
sendToEvm(...)
Initiate a
transfer from Core to EVM
.
The following methods accept calls only from
L1InteropManager
.
Method
Requested Core operation
registerDeposit(...)
Credit an
L1 deposit
.
registerL1NativeAssetOnCore(...)
,
registerEvmNativeAssetOnCore(...)
,
registerCoreNativeAssetOnCore(...)
Register an asset on Core. See
Registering on Core
for L1-native and EVM-native assets.
finalizeEvmWrapperLink(...)
Record the
EVM wrapper
for an L1-native asset.
finalizeL1WrapperLink(...)
Record the
L1 wrapper
for an EVM-native asset.
L1CoreMessaging
also exposes
setSystemConfig(...)
,
updateAsset(...)
,
createMarket(...)
, and
updateMarket(...)
for governance-authorized callers. These submit protocol-configuration requests through the same queue.
Core to L1
Core emits
L1 Calls
in the following cases.
Processing
withdrawals to L1
.
Returning
unaccepted L1 deposit amounts
.
Confirming an
EVM-native token link
.
These
L1 Calls
are included in a batch. Once that batch has been
executed on L1
, anyone can call the bridge to execute them.
For Core-originated
L1 Calls
,
l2Sender
is always the
Core system address
.
Executing Core messages on L1
Once the batch containing the call has been executed on L1, retrieve the call data from Core using
GET /api/v1/coreL1Call?tx_hash=...
. Set
CORE_API_URL
to your network's Core API URL and
CORE_TX_HASH
to the hash of the Core transaction that generated the call.
For operations initiated on L1 or EVM, obtain
CORE_TX_HASH
as follows.
From L1.
Look up the initiating L1 transaction with
GET /api/v1/txFromL1TxHash?hash=...
and use the returned Core transaction's
hash
field.
From EVM.
Derive the Core transaction hash
from the request's
WriteToCore
event.
Request
Response (example)
curl --get "$CORE_API_URL/api/v1/coreL1Call" \
  --data-urlencode "tx_hash=$CORE_TX_HASH" | jq
{
  "code": 200,
  "call": {
    "l2_sender": "0x7fffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff",
    "target": "0x...",
    "value": "0",
    "msg_nonce": "42",
    "calldata": "0x...",
    "l1_call_hash": "0x..."
  }
}
The response's
call
object contains the arguments needed to execute the
L1 Call
through
ZkLighter.executeCoreL1Call(...)
. Submit them once the batch has been executed on L1.
Call data may be available before batch execution. The API does not report whether the
L1 Call
has already been executed.
Solidity
function executeCoreL1Call(
    address _l2Sender,
    address to,
    uint256 value,
    uint256 msgNonce,
    bytes calldata data
) external;
The bridge checks that the call belongs to an executed batch and has not already been executed.
During execution, the target can read the authenticated cross-domain sender through the bridge's
l2Sender()
function. To authenticate a Core-originated
L1 Call
, the target
MUST
check the following.
msg.sender
is the address of the
ZkLighter
bridge.
ZkLighter.l2Sender()
equals the
Core system address
.
If
executeCoreL1Call(...)
fails, it can be retried. Once it succeeds, the same
L1 Call
cannot be executed again. The transaction sender pays the L1 gas fees but cannot alter the message itself.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
The L1 bridge
ZkLighter
intermediates messaging between L1 and Lighter EVM.
Arbitrary cross-domain messaging is supported between the two domains.
L1 to EVM
L1 accounts can submit transactions to Lighter EVM through the bridge's EVM priority queue. The EVM sequencer processes these requests asynchronously in first-in, first-out order.
For example, a caller can request
setValue(42)
on an EVM contract by setting
to
to the target address and encoding the call in
data
.
Submitting an EVM priority request
Call
ZkLighter.addEvmPriorityRequest(...)
on L1 to submit a request.
Solidity
function addEvmPriorityRequest(
    address to,
    uint256 value,
    uint256 depositAmount,
    uint256 gasLimit,
    bool isCreation,
    address refundAddress,
    bytes memory data
) external payable;
The parameters define the transaction to execute on Lighter EVM.
address to
is the target of the EVM transaction.
uint256 value
is the amount of ETH to send to the target with the transaction on EVM. It comes out of the sender's EVM balance after
depositAmount
is credited, so a sender with no EVM balance must set
depositAmount
to at least
value
.
uint256 depositAmount
is the amount of ETH to deposit on EVM for the (potentially aliased)
msg.sender
. Once the priority request is accepted on L1, this amount is
guaranteed
to be credited to that EVM address, even if the EVM transaction fails.
uint256 gasLimit
is the gas limit for the EVM transaction.
bool isCreation
selects whether the transaction is a contract-creation transaction. If
true
,
to
must be
address(0)
and
data
must contain the creation bytecode, including any encoded constructor arguments.
address refundAddress
is the address on L1 that will receive any excess
msg.value
after fees and the deposit amount are deducted.
bytes memory data
is the transaction's calldata, or its initialization code when
isCreation
is
true
.
msg.value
must cover at least the
priority request fee
plus
depositAmount
. Any excess is refunded to
refundAddress
. The fee is forwarded to the protocol treasury.
A successful L1 transaction confirms submission, not successful execution on EVM.
Priority request fee calculation
Estimate the fee by calling
computePriorityFee(gasLimit)
on the
ZkLighter
bridge with the gas limit you plan to request.
Solidity
function computePriorityFee(uint256 gasLimit) public view returns (uint256);
The fee depends on the base fee (
block.basefee
) and blob base fee (
block.blobbasefee
) of the L1 block that includes the request. These can change before inclusion, so add a buffer to the estimate and send it along with
depositAmount
. Any
msg.value
above the actual fee plus
depositAmount
is refunded to
refundAddress
.
The fee itself is charged in full and is not refunded for unused execution gas or pubdata.
When quoting with
eth_call
, explicitly set a nonzero
gasPrice
at least as high as the selected L1 block's base fee. Otherwise, the node can execute the call with
block.basefee
set to zero and underestimate the fee. No block override is needed to use the selected block's base fee and blob base fee.
With
cast
, pin the quote to the latest block and read its base fee.
Bash
quote_block=$(cast block-number --rpc-url "$L1_RPC_URL")
quote_base_fee=$(cast basefee "$quote_block" --rpc-url "$L1_RPC_URL")
QUOTE_CALLER=0x000000000000000000000000000000000000dEaD
REQUEST_GAS_LIMIT=200000

cast call "$ZK_LIGHTER_BRIDGE" \
  'computePriorityFee(uint256)(uint256)' "$REQUEST_GAS_LIMIT" \
  --rpc-url "$L1_RPC_URL" \
  --block "$quote_block" \
  --from "$QUOTE_CALLER" \
  --legacy \
  --gas-price "$((quote_base_fee + 1))" \
  --gas-limit 100000 \
  --override-balance "$QUOTE_CALLER:1000000000000000000"
As in the example, you may also need to override the caller's balance to satisfy the simulation's gas-payment check. This does not fund the account on-chain or spend ETH. Here,
--gas-limit
limits the fee-quote call itself;
REQUEST_GAS_LIMIT
is the gas requested for the EVM priority transaction.
msg.sender
of the EVM priority transaction
To prevent contract-address spoofing, contract-senders of EVM priority transactions are aliased on Lighter EVM using the following rule.
Solidity
uint160 constant OFFSET = uint160(0x1111000000000000000000000000000000001111);

function _applyL1ToL2Alias(address sender) internal pure returns (address l2Address) {
    /// @solidity memory-safe-assembly
    unchecked {
        l2Address = address(uint160(sender) + OFFSET);
    }
}
Whether aliasing applies is determined at runtime by the L1 check
msg.sender != tx.origin
. EIP-7702 accounts can choose to trigger or avoid aliasing depending on how they submit the request.
The EVM target can authenticate the expected L1 caller as follows.
EOA sender without aliasing.
Check
msg.sender == expectedL1Sender
.
Contract-sender with aliasing.
Undo the alias before comparing the resulting address with the expected L1 sender.
Solidity
function _undoL1ToL2Alias(address sender) internal pure returns (address l1Address) {
    unchecked {
        l1Address = address(uint160(sender) - OFFSET);
    }
}
Finding the corresponding L2 transaction
Each EVM priority request produces exactly one L2 transaction. Its hash is deterministic, so you can compute it from the corresponding event in the L1 transaction receipt.
Decode the
NewEvmPriorityRequest
event emitted by the L1 bridge
ZkLighter
. It has the following fields.
Solidity
event NewEvmPriorityRequest(
    uint64 indexed requestId,
    address indexed sender,
    address indexed to,
    uint256 mintAmount,
    uint256 value,
    uint256 gasLimit,
    bool isCreation,
    bytes data,
    uint64 expirationTimestamp,
    bytes32 prefixHash
);
Compute
sourceHash = keccak256(prefixHash)
, hashing the 32 raw bytes of the event's
prefixHash
.
RLP-encode the fields in the order shown below, prepend the single transaction-type byte
0x7E
, then hash the resulting bytes.
Text
l2TxHash = keccak256(0x7E || rlp([
  uint8(1), sourceHash, sender, to, mintAmount, value, gasLimit, isCreation, data
]))
Failure model
An EVM priority request is consumed when its transaction is processed, even if the transaction reverts. Reversion undoes the EVM call's effects, including any transfer of
value
to the target, but does not undo the initiating L1 transaction or the
depositAmount
credited to the sender's EVM address. The request is not retryable.
Some protocols need the EVM action to succeed after an operation has already completed on L1. For example, tokens locked on L1 may still need to be minted on EVM after a failed first attempt. For stronger delivery guarantees, use
L1ReplayableMessenger
to make the message retryable while preventing duplicate successful execution.
L1ReplayableMessenger
L1ReplayableMessenger
builds on the EVM priority queue and relays messages through
EvmReplayableMessenger
on EVM. Together, they handle replayability and abstract away sender aliasing for applications.
To initiate a replayable message, call
sendMessage(...)
on L1 with the target and encoded call. Make sure to supply the appropriate
priority request fee
along with
value
as
msg.value
. Any excess is returned to
refundAddress
.
Solidity
function sendMessage(
    address target,
    bytes calldata message,
    uint256 gasLimit,
    uint256 value,
    address refundAddress
) external payable;
If delivery fails, anyone can call
replayMessage(...)
on L1 with the original message fields and a new gas limit. Each retry submits a new priority request and pays a fresh priority fee.
Solidity
function replayMessage(
    address _from,
    address _to,
    uint256 _value,
    uint256 _messageNonce,
    address _refundAddress,
    bytes memory _message,
    uint32 _newGasLimit
) external payable;
_from
is the original caller of
L1ReplayableMessenger.sendMessage(...)
, without aliasing. For a gateway transfer, this is the gateway contract.
_to
is the original
target
address on EVM.
_value
is the original
value
, in wei. The retry's
msg.value
only needs to cover the new
priority request fee
.
_messageNonce
is the original submission's
NewEvmPriorityRequest.requestId
. Reuse it on every retry, even though each retry creates a new priority request.
_refundAddress
is the L1 address that receives any excess fee payment for this retry. It may differ from the original refund address.
_message
is the original
message
calldata passed to
sendMessage(...)
.
_newGasLimit
is the gas limit for the new EVM relay transaction. It can be increased for the retry.
Recover
_from
,
_to
,
_messageNonce
, and
_message
by decoding
relayMessage(...)
from the original
NewEvmPriorityRequest
event's
data
field. Use that event's
value
field for
_value
.
A failed relay leaves the message available for another attempt. Once the target call succeeds, the same message cannot execute again. Replayability does not guarantee eventual success if the target continues to revert.
At the target,
msg.sender
is
EvmReplayableMessenger
, not the original L1 sender or its alias. For authentication purposes, the target should check both conditions.
msg.sender == address(EVM_REPLAYABLE_MESSENGER)
, using the
EvmReplayableMessenger
predeploy
.
EVM_REPLAYABLE_MESSENGER.xDomainSender() == expectedL1Sender
, where
expectedL1Sender
is the authorized L1 address.
Circumventing Core sequencer censorship for EVM-controlled Core accounts
An EOA controlling an EVM-controlled Core account can use an
L1-to-EVM priority request
to submit a Core operation without relying on ordinary transaction submission to the sequencer. Call
ZkLighter.addEvmPriorityRequest(...)
directly from that EOA on L1, with
to
set to
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
and
data
encoding a supported operation such as
cancelAllOrders(accountIndex)
. A direct EOA call preserves the controller's address as
msg.sender
on EVM.
The sequencer is required to process the EVM priority request. Successful execution on EVM submits the write for Core to fulfill asynchronously. Both the priority request and the resulting Core write are covered by the protocol's
escape-hatch conditions
, so prolonged censorship at either stage allows anyone to activate the escape hatch.
For a contract-controlled Core account, route the priority request through the controlling EVM contract so that it submits the Core write.
EVM to L1
Initiating an L1 Call
EVM-originated
L1 Calls
pass through the
EvmToL1Messenger
predeploy
. It supports
arbitrary calls
and
token-info reports
.
Arbitrary calls
To initiate an arbitrary
L1 Call
, call
initiateWithdrawal(...)
with the target address and calldata.
Solidity
function initiateWithdrawal(
    address _target,
    bytes memory _data
) public payable;
Parameters:
_target
is the address of the L1 contract to call.
_data
is the calldata for the L1 call.
Implicit inputs:
msg.sender
— Exposed to L1 (transiently) as the initiator of the withdrawal.
msg.value
— The amount of ETH to withdraw from Lighter EVM. If nonzero, the ETH is burned on the EVM side via a
selfdestruct
-based burner contract.
A successful call to
initiateWithdrawal
emits the following event:
Solidity
enum WithdrawalKind { User, SendTokenInfo }

event WithdrawalInitiated(
    address indexed sender,
    address indexed to,
    uint256 value,
    uint256 nonce,
    WithdrawalKind kind,
    bytes data
);
Field
Description
sender
The initiator of the withdrawal on Lighter EVM (
msg.sender
).
to
The
_target
passed to
initiateWithdrawal
.
value
The
msg.value
sent with the call.
nonce
A monotonically incrementing counter tracking the total number of EVM withdrawals, maintained by the
EvmToL1Messenger
.
kind
User
for calls initiated through
initiateWithdrawal(...)
.
Token-info reports
use
SendTokenInfo
.
data
The
_data
passed to
initiateWithdrawal
.
Token-info reports
Anyone can call
EvmInteropManager.sendTokenInfo(...)
to request a token-info report for an EVM token.
Solidity
function sendTokenInfo(address evmToken) external;
The resulting
L1 Call
targets
L1InteropManager
and carries the token's ERC-20 metadata and a protocol-supplied admin-slot value. The underlying
EvmToL1Messenger.sendTokenInfo(...)
method accepts calls only from
EvmInteropManager
.
See
Token linking
for the requirements and full workflow.
Executing the call on L1
As with
Core-originated
L1 Calls
, EVM-originated
L1 Calls
become available for execution on L1 once their
batch has been executed
.
However, unlike Core-originated calls, EVM-originated
L1 Calls
are committed to on L1 through a Merkle root. Executing one therefore requires a Merkle proof of its inclusion in the batch, as outlined below.
Obtaining the proof
Lighter EVM nodes provide the proof and all execution arguments through
lighter_getWithdrawalProof
. Call this JSON-RPC method on the Lighter EVM RPC endpoint:
lighter_getWithdrawalProof(txHash, index)
Parameters:
Parameter
Description
txHash
Hash of the Lighter EVM transaction that emitted the
WithdrawalInitiated
event.
index
Zero-based position of the
WithdrawalInitiated
event among those emitted by that transaction.
0
unless the transaction initiated several withdrawals.
For example, using
curl
:
Bash
curl -s "$LIGHTER_EVM_RPC_URL" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"lighter_getWithdrawalProof","params":["0x<l2 tx hash>", 0]}'
The response contains the Merkle proof and all arguments of the L1 claim:
JSON
{
  "batchNumber": 1287,
  "proof": [
    "0x9d2f…",
    "0x41c0…"
  ],
  "isLeft": "0x2",
  "l1CallHash": "0x7b3e…",
  "root": "0xe5a1…",
  "l2Sender": "0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266",
  "to": "0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266",
  "value": "0x2386f26fc10000",
  "msgNonce": "0x1c",
  "data": "0x"
}
Response fields:
Field
Description
batchNumber
The finalized batch that contains the withdrawal. First argument of
executeEvmL1Call
.
proof
The Merkle proof. Empty when the batch contains a single withdrawal.
isLeft
Position of the withdrawal in the batch's Merkle tree, as a hex quantity. Pass it as
uint256
.
l1CallHash
Hash of the withdrawal message.
root
The batch's Merkle root.
l2Sender
,
to
,
value
,
msgNonce
,
data
The committed
L1 Call
fields used for execution.
Until the withdrawal has been finalized on L1, the method returns an error. Retry after a few seconds.
Submitting the claim
Call
executeEvmL1Call
on the
ZkLighter
bridge contract on L1:
Solidity
function executeEvmL1Call(
    uint64 batchNumber,
    bytes32[] calldata proof,
    uint256 isLeft,
    address _l2Sender,
    address to,
    uint256 value,
    uint256 msgNonce,
    bytes calldata data
) external;
Parameter
Source
Description
batchNumber
proof
The finalized batch that contains the withdrawal.
proof
proof
The Merkle proof.
isLeft
proof
Position of the withdrawal in the batch's Merkle tree.
_l2Sender
proof
l2Sender
The call's authenticated EVM sender. Surfaced via
l2Sender()
during execution.
to
proof
to
The target of the L1 call.
value
proof

The amount of ETH sent with the call.
msgNonce
proof

The nonce of the withdrawal, as tracked by the
EvmToL1Messenger
.
data

The calldata for the L1 call.
All eight arguments are contained in the response of
lighter_getWithdrawalProof
.
Anyone can submit the claim; it is not submitted automatically. The ETH and calldata are delivered to
to
, and the submitter pays the L1 gas.
During execution, the target contract must authenticate the calling bridge before reading the original EVM sender through
l2Sender()
.
Solidity
function l2Sender() external view returns (address sender);
The
_l2Sender
is stored transiently and is only available for the duration of the call.
If the downstream call reverts, the entire
executeEvmL1Call
transaction reverts and the withdrawal remains unclaimed, so it can be retried with the same proof. Each withdrawal can be claimed only once. Simulating the call with
eth_call
before sending it surfaces the revert reason and confirms that the withdrawal is claimable.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.title: Reading Core from EVM
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
EVM contracts can read Core state synchronously through the
READ_CORE
precompile
. Each read completes within the calling transaction and returns its result directly.
For each EVM block, the sequencer selects one sealed Core block (called the
parent Core block
) and pins its post-execution state for all Core reads in that EVM block. This keeps read results consistent throughout the EVM block, even if the selected snapshot lags the Core tip.
The
READ_CORE
precompile charges 20,000 gas per call, plus any memory expansion costs.
Execution
An EVM contract reads Core state by calling the
READ_CORE
precompile
with an encoded query. The read completes synchronously and returns its result within the same call. Reads can also be evaluated off-chain through
eth_call
.
📘
Note
eth_call
s that perform
READ_CORE
only succeed with the
latest
block tag. Support for earlier blocks is planned for an upcoming update.
Reads have no request ID, do not enter a queue, and require no destination transaction. They neither modify Core state nor record a request on Core.
Reads use the pinned snapshot rather than the latest Core state. Consequently:
The same read in a later EVM block can return a different result if that block uses a newer Core snapshot.
Reads do not reflect writes submitted earlier in the same EVM block, including within the same transaction.
A
transaction-status read
returns status
0
if the request was unprocessed in this Core snapshot, even if the Core tip has processed it since.
Failures
A failed read consumes all gas forwarded to
READ_CORE
and returns no data. In Solidity,
call
and
staticcall
report the failure by returning
false
.
Reads fail for unsupported selectors, malformed input, insufficient gas, or unmet query requirements—for example, a requested account, asset, or market that does not exist.
Supported reads
Selector
Read
Description

Processing status and result of an EVM-initiated Core write.

Position, margin, and order information for an account and market.

Reads that take a controlling address resolve to its master account, so subaccounts cannot be read.

Example: reading a spot balance
The following contract reads a Core spot balance.
Solidity
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract CoreReader {
    address constant READ_CORE = 0x6600000000000000000000000000000000000000;

    function spotBalance(
        address accountAddress,
        bool isL1Account,
        uint32 assetId
    ) external view returns (int128 availableBalance, int128 lockedBalance) {
        (bool success, bytes memory result) = READ_CORE.staticcall(
            abi.encodePacked(uint16(0x0006), accountAddress, isL1Account, assetId)
        );
        require(success, "Core balance read failed");
        return abi.decode(result, (int128, int128));
    }
}

Message passing

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
📘
Note
This page is for governance and token admins who register and link assets.
Asset registration requires governance action. To get an asset registered on the devnet, reach out to the Lighter team.
Lighter supports assets whose native domain is Ethereum L1, Lighter EVM, or Lighter Core. Token linking connects tokens on their native domain to tokens on their non-native domains.
Canonical domain
L1 representation
EVM representation
Core representation
L1
Canonical ERC-20
Wrapped ERC-20
Wrapped Core balance
EVM
Wrapped ERC-20
Canonical ERC-20
Wrapped Core balance
Core
None
None
Native Core asset
Token linking is not supported for Core-native assets, which have no representation on L1 or Lighter EVM. The rest of this page therefore covers L1-native and EVM-native ERC-20 assets.
ETH is linked across all three domains by default and requires no ERC-20 linking flow.
Flow at a glance
L1-native asset
Register.
Governance
registers the asset on L1, then on Core. See
L1-native assets
.
Add the EVM wrapper (optional).
The Core token admin initiates wrapper setup from L1. EVM deploys or verifies the wrapper. See
Select the EVM wrapper
.
A custom EVM wrapper token requires
proof of control
.
EVM-native asset
Register.
Governance
registers the asset on L1, then on Core. See
EVM-native assets
.
Prove control.
Set the canonical EVM token's admin slot to the Core token admin's address, then send its token-info report from EVM and execute it on L1 before linking. See
Proving control of an EVM token
.
Link the canonical token.
The Core token admin initiates linking from L1. Wait for EVM and Core to record the token, then execute Core's confirmation on L1. See
Linking the canonical token
.
Add the L1 wrapper (optional).
The Core token admin initiates wrapper setup from L1, which deploys or verifies the L1 wrapper. See
Select the L1 wrapper
.
A custom L1 wrapper token requires
proof of control
.
Linking makes an asset transferable. Trading it on Core also needs a market, which governance creates separately.
Roles
There are two privileged roles that manage a token's linking lifecycle through the
L1InteropManager
contract on L1.
Governance
registers assets on Core and appoints their Core token admins. Governance also approves control of custom L1 wrapper tokens, see
Proving control of an L1 token
for details.
The Core token admin
(
coreTokenAdmin
) is an L1 address that governance records for each asset at registration. It is the only address that can initiate token linking and wrapper setup for that asset. Governance can change the Core token admin after registration.
Proving control of tokens
Before a
coreTokenAdmin
may associate a Core asset with an independently deployed token contract, it must prove control of that contract. This prevents a malicious Core token admin from claiming a token it does not own and thereby blocking the token's true owner from later linking it to the correct Core asset.
How control is proved depends on whether the token contract is on L1 or Lighter EVM.
Proving control of an EVM token
On Lighter EVM, a token contract signals its controller by storing the controller's address in a protocol-defined storage slot.
The
EvmInteropManager
can then send the slot value, together with the token's ERC-20 metadata, to
L1InteropManager
, which coordinates token-linking authorization and management on L1. When the token is proposed for linking, the reported controller is compared with the Core asset's
coreTokenAdmin
. The values must match before the link is authorized.
The detailed execution steps are described below.
Step 1.
Set the token's admin slot to the asset's
coreTokenAdmin
address. The admin slot is:
Solidity
// keccak256("lighter.admin.slot")
bytes32 constant TOKEN_ADMIN_SLOT =
    0x4d2e8bd502eb517f6a9601bbafcec9c20dec0101dc1413f43ae2900ce65ed098;
Store the address in the low 20 bytes of the slot. The upper 12 bytes must be zero. Before the asset is registered, use the address governance will appoint as
coreTokenAdmin
.
Step 2.
On Lighter EVM, call
EvmInteropManager.sendTokenInfo(evmToken)
, where
evmToken
is the address of the EVM token being linked. Anyone can make this call.
Solidity
function sendTokenInfo(address evmToken) external;
The token-info report includes the token's admin slot value at the end of the reporting EVM block and its ERC-20 name, symbol, and decimals. If
name()
or
symbol()
is missing, the report uses an empty string for that field. If
decimals()
is missing, it uses
18
. Each report is independent, and reports do not have to execute on L1 in EVM submission order. Executing a report overwrites the admin and metadata stored by an earlier report.
Step 3.
Execute
the resulting token-info report on L1. This records the token's admin address and metadata in
L1InteropManager
.
Step 4.
Verify the recorded admin by calling
L1InteropManager.evmApprovedTokenAdmin(evmToken)
on L1. It must return the asset's
coreTokenAdmin
address.
Proving control of an L1 token
Unlike on Lighter EVM, the protocol cannot directly inspect an arbitrary L1 token's storage to verify who controls it. Governance therefore acts as the trusted attestor and records the address authorized to link each L1 token contract.
Step 1.
Request that governance call
L1InteropManager.setL1ApprovedTokenAdmin(l1Token, coreTokenAdmin)
on L1.
Solidity
function setL1ApprovedTokenAdmin(address token, address admin) external;
Only governance can make this call. Pass the L1 token address as
token
and the asset's
coreTokenAdmin
address as
admin
.
Step 2.
Query
L1InteropManager.l1ApprovedTokenAdmin(l1Token)
on L1. It must return the asset's
coreTokenAdmin
address.
Registering on Core
Registering an asset on Core enables transfers between Core and the asset's canonical domain. For an EVM-native asset, the canonical EVM token must also be linked before those transfers become available.
Governance
registers an asset in two calls on
L1InteropManager
:
Store the L1 configuration.
This call records:
uint32 assetIndex
, the asset identifier.
address coreTokenAdmin
, the Core token admin's address.
uint128 tickSize
, how many of the token's smallest EVM units make up one
Core base unit
; see
Amounts
.
uint56 extensionMultiplier
, Lighter's internal asset extension multiplier.
For an L1-native asset, the canonical L1 token address.
Create the asset on Core.
This submits a priority request that creates the asset on Core with its Core-side parameters, such as symbol, minimum transfer and withdrawal amounts, and margin mode.
Core registration is a cross-domain request and can be retried if it fails. Linking cannot complete until Core has registered the asset.
L1-native assets
Governance
calls
registerL1NativeAssetConfig
, then
registerL1NativeAssetOnCore
. Registration records the canonical L1 token address, so transfers between L1 and Core are available as soon as Core registration succeeds. No further linking is needed for that path.
EVM-native assets
Governance
calls
registerEvmNativeAssetConfig
, then
registerEvmNativeAssetOnCore
. These calls create the asset on Core but do not associate it with an EVM token. To complete EVM-native registration, the Core token admin links the canonical token and waits for Core to record it.
Linking the canonical token
Step 1.
Complete the governance calls for
EVM-native registration
.
Step 2.
Ensure you have
proved control of the EVM token
, including delivery of its token-info report to L1.
Step 3.
On L1, call
L1InteropManager.linkEvmNativeToken
as
coreTokenAdmin
.
Solidity
function linkEvmNativeToken(
    uint32 assetIndex,
    address evmToken,
    uint256 gasLimit
) external payable;
Type
Parameter
Description
uint32
assetIndex
Index of the registered EVM-native Core asset.
address
evmToken
Address of the canonical EVM token whose approved admin matches
coreTokenAdmin
.
uint256
gasLimit
Gas limit for the EVM token-linking transaction.
Step 4.
Wait for EVM to record the token and notify Core. Query
EvmInteropManager.getAssetConfig(assetIndex)
and confirm that its
evmToken
field matches the canonical EVM token address.
Step 5.
Wait for Core to record the token and create its confirmation call to L1. Query Core's
EVM token address
and confirm that it equals
evmToken
.
Step 6.
Execute the
Core-to-L1 confirmation
. Confirm that
L1InteropManager.evmNativeLinkedToken(assetIndex)
equals
evmToken
before adding an L1 wrapper.
Enabling the external wrapper — gateway selection
The final (optional) step in the token linking life cycle enables the wrapper on the external domain opposite the canonical token: EVM for an L1-native asset, or L1 for an EVM-native asset. This process is called gateway selection.
Gateway selection chooses the external wrapper token and two gateway contracts, one on the canonical domain and one on the wrapped-token domain. The contract on the canonical domain takes custody of the underlying tokens, while the contract on the other domain manages the selected wrapper. For example, an EVM-native asset uses an escrow contract on Lighter EVM, called the
escrow gateway
, and a minting contract on L1, called the
mint gateway
. These counterpart contracts form a
gateway pair
and are selected together.
L1InteropManager
and
EvmInteropManager
do not manage the wrapper token directly. They operate it through the selected gateways using standard interfaces. The mint gateway holds whatever permissions the wrapper requires for minting and burning, rather than granting those permissions to
L1InteropManager
or
EvmInteropManager
.
The gateways may also use the cross-domain messaging system to support transfers directly between L1 and Lighter EVM, independently of Core. Notably, the gateways (and therefore that bridge) can exist before the token is registered on Core and before
L1InteropManager
and/or
EvmInteropManager
become aware of it. As long as the gateways adhere to the appropriate interfaces, gateway selection can later connect the existing custody and wrapper system to the Core asset.
The
default gateways
provide an example of a gateway pair that enables this direct L1–EVM bridge.
Transfers between Core and the canonical domain do not require gateways. They become available once the
registration process
is complete.
After registration, but before gateway selection, deposits from the canonical domain into Core are escrowed by
L1InteropManager
for L1-native assets or
EvmInteropManager
for EVM-native assets. An independently operating L1–EVM bridge holds its escrow in its own gateway.
During gateway selection, any canonical tokens held by
L1InteropManager
or
EvmInteropManager
move to the selected escrow gateway, delegating custody of the tokens to the gateways.
Gateway requirements
Every gateway selected for Core integration must implement the interfaces below so that
L1InteropManager
and
EvmInteropManager
can interact with it. The Core token admin is responsible for selecting compatible contracts—it may use the protocol's
default gateways
or implement and deploy its own pair.
A gateway pair must preserve the asset's backing invariant—the canonical tokens held by the escrow gateway must cover the asset's combined representations on Core and the wrapped-token domain.
The interfaces define only the behavior required for Core integration. Gateways may provide additional functionality, such as direct transfers between L1 and Lighter EVM. Because the contracts exist independently of Core, a gateway pair may be deployed before or after the Core asset is created. Gateway selection can later connect an existing pair to the Core asset.
Gateway interfaces
The gateway on the canonical domain implements
IEscrowGateway
:
Solidity
interface IEscrowGateway {
    function externalGateway() external view returns (address);
    function unlock(address localToken, address to, uint256 amount) external;
}
externalGateway()
returns the address of the paired mint gateway on the other domain: EVM for an L1 escrow gateway, or L1 for an EVM escrow gateway.
unlock(localToken, to, amount)
transfers
amount
of the canonical token at
localToken
from the gateway's escrow to the recipient
to
.
The gateway on the wrapped-token domain implements
IMintGateway
:
Solidity
interface IMintGateway {
    function externalGateway() external view returns (address);
    function checkOrDeployToken(
        bytes32 salt,
        string calldata name,
        string calldata symbol,
        uint8 decimals
    ) external;
    function mint(address localToken, address to, uint256 amount, bytes calldata data) external;
    function managerBurn(address localToken, uint256 amount) external;
}
externalGateway()
returns the address of the paired escrow gateway on the other domain: EVM for an L1 mint gateway, or L1 for an EVM mint gateway.
checkOrDeployToken(...)
must ensure the selected wrapper exists. The supplied
salt
is
bytes32(uint256(uint160(canonicalToken)))
.
L1InteropManager
or
EvmInteropManager
calls this function during gateway selection, after the canonical token has been successfully linked to the Core asset. The manager derives the
salt
from the canonical token in the authenticated asset configuration, so the gateway can treat it as a protocol-authenticated identifier within its canonical-domain namespace and safely use it for deterministic CREATE2 or CREATE3 wrapper deployment, if desired.
mint(...)
mints wrapped tokens to the recipient.
managerBurn(...)
is called by
L1InteropManager
on L1 or
EvmInteropManager
on Lighter EVM after that contract transfers the wrapped tokens directly from the user to the mint gateway. The function burns those tokens from the gateway's balance.
The gateway must allow
managerBurn(...)
calls from
L1InteropManager
on L1 or
EvmInteropManager
on Lighter EVM. Whether to reject calls from other addresses is up to the gateway designer.
For
unlock(...)
and
mint(...)
, allow calls from
L1InteropManager
on L1 and
EvmInteropManager
on Lighter EVM.
External wrapper requirements
Before selecting a custom wrapper, establish that the
coreTokenAdmin
controls it. For an EVM wrapper, set the protocol-defined admin slot and deliver it to L1 by calling
sendTokenInfo(...)
. For an L1 wrapper,
governance records the approved admin
.
The protocol also supplies the canonical token's
name()
,
symbol()
, and
decimals()
to the mint gateway through
checkOrDeployToken(...)
. For an EVM-native token, these values are recorded by
sendTokenInfo(...)
. For an L1-native token,
L1InteropManager
reads them during gateway selection. A missing
name()
or
symbol()
produces an empty string, and a missing
decimals()
produces
18
. The wrapper should use the same decimals as the canonical token because gateway operations pass token amounts between domains without conversion.
Default gateways
The default gateways are a protocol-provided special case of gateway pairs. They implement the same gateway interfaces and satisfy the
gateway requirements
. Unlike a custom pair, their wrapper deployment behavior is fixed by the protocol.
Each default mint gateway uses CREATE2 to deploy a wrapper backed by a protocol-configured
LighterWrappedERC20V1
implementation. The wrapper is initialized with the canonical token's
name()
,
symbol()
, and
decimals()
without adding a prefix or suffix. A missing
name()
or
symbol()
produces an empty string, and a missing
decimals()
produces
18
.
If the wrapper does not yet exist, the transaction that deploys it must have enough gas for both
CREATE2
and
initialize(...)
, in addition to the rest of the operation. For deployment through an EVM priority request, include these costs in its
gasLimit
: a delivery that deploys a default EVM wrapper uses about 450,000 gas.
Default wrappers are upgradeable, and all wrappers deployed by a given mint gateway share the same implementation.
The deployed protocol contracts recognize the default
L1 gateway addresses
and
EVM gateway addresses
. Passing those addresses during gateway selection selects this known deployment path, allowing the protocol to derive and verify the wrapper address instead of requiring proof that the Core token admin controls it. The wrapper can therefore bypass the proof-of-control protocol.
The protocol provides the following default gateway implementations:
Asset
L1 gateway
EVM gateway
L1-native
DefaultL1EscrowGateway
DefaultEvmMintGateway
EVM-native
DefaultL1MintGateway
DefaultEvmEscrowGateway
The default gateway pairs also support direct L1–EVM bridging. If you want users to bridge between L1 and EVM before the Core asset exists, and you intend to use the default gateways for its eventual Core integration, you can direct users to the default gateway pair immediately. The Core asset can be registered and linked to the same pair later.
For L1-to-EVM transfers, the default gateways use
L1ReplayableMessenger
. Failed delivery can be retried, but each message can execute successfully only once.
Selecting the gateway pair
Enable an EVM wrapper for an L1-native asset
During gateway selection,
L1InteropManager
reads the L1 token's metadata and passes it to the selected EVM mint gateway through
checkOrDeployToken(...)
. Missing metadata fields use the fallbacks described above. The protocol treats this metadata as stable and does not synchronize changes to a wrapper that already exists, including one deployed before gateway selection.
Prerequisites.
Complete
L1-native registration
. If using a custom EVM wrapper, also complete its
proof of control
.
Step 1.
Choose the gateway pair and
expectedEvmWrapperToken
. With defaults, read
EvmMintGateway.computeTokenAddress(l1Token)
on EVM. With custom gateways, pass the appropriate wrapper token address.
Step 2.
On L1, call
L1InteropManager.selectL1NativeGatewayPair
as
coreTokenAdmin
with the selected EVM mint and L1 escrow gateway addresses. For defaults, use
EvmMintGateway
and
L1EscrowGateway
at the addresses listed in
Chain Info
.
Solidity
function selectL1NativeGatewayPair(
    uint32 assetIndex,
    address evmGateway,
    address l1Gateway,
    address expectedEvmWrapperToken,
    uint256 gasLimit
) external payable;
Type
Parameter
Description
uint32
assetIndex
Index of the registered L1-native Core asset.
address
evmGateway
Address of the EVM mint gateway.
address
l1Gateway
Address of the L1 escrow gateway.
address
expectedEvmWrapperToken
Expected EVM wrapper address; must match the default mint gateway's computed address when using defaults.
uint256
gasLimit
Gas limit for the EVM gateway-selection transaction.
Step 3.
Wait for EVM to deploy or verify the wrapper. Query
EvmInteropManager.getAssetConfig(assetIndex)
and confirm that its
evmToken
field equals
expectedEvmWrapperToken
.
Step 4.
Execute the
acknowledgment on L1
. This finalizes the L1 gateway, moves any existing escrow into it, and notifies Core of the EVM wrapper.
Step 5.
Wait for Core to record the wrapper. Query Core's
EVM token address
and confirm that it equals
expectedEvmWrapperToken

Enable an L1 wrapper for an EVM-native asset
During
EVM-native registration
,
sendTokenInfo(...)
reports the canonical EVM token's
name()
,
symbol()
, and
decimals()
to L1. Each executed report overwrites metadata previously stored by
L1InteropManager
. Gateway selection passes the stored snapshot to the selected L1 mint gateway through
checkOrDeployToken(...)
. Later reports or metadata changes do not update an already deployed wrapper.
Prerequisites.
Complete
EVM-native registration
. If using a custom L1 wrapper, also complete its
governance approval
.
Step 1.
Choose the gateway pair and
expectedL1WrapperToken
. With defaults, read
L1MintGateway.computeTokenAddress(evmToken)
on L1. With custom gateways, pass the appropriate wrapper token address.
Step 2.
On L1, call
L1InteropManager.selectEvmNativeGatewayPair
as
coreTokenAdmin
with the selected EVM escrow and L1 mint gateway addresses. For defaults, use
EvmEscrowGateway
and
L1MintGateway
at the addresses listed in
Chain Info
. This call deploys or verifies the L1 wrapper using the previously reported token metadata.

This section covers how to transfer assets between Ethereum L1, Lighter EVM, and Lighter Core. These transfers build on the cross-domain pathways introduced in
Message passing
.
Transfers to and from Core
The following conventions apply to transfers between
EVM and Core
and
L1 and Core
.
Supported assets
Every asset on Core is identified by a
uint32 assetIndex
.
Transfers to and from Core support the following asset types.
ETH.
ETH uses
assetIndex = 1
and is transferred as the native currency on L1 and Lighter EVM.
ERC-20 tokens.
The asset must be registered on Core and linked on the relevant non-Core domain. See
Token linking
.
If a Core asset has representations on both L1 and Lighter EVM, the protocol assumes they use the same number of decimals.
The following assets are currently registered on Core.
Asset
assetIndex
L1 / EVM decimals
tickSize
L1 address
EVM address
ETH
1
18
10^10
Not applicable
Not applicable
LIT
2
18
10^10
0x24734C47a5967b3ab43eC137909BcF72593E65E8
Not linked
USDC
3
6
1
0xb90a9f16ddf0AE8054d53AF5C8b559a19741991F
0xf2A5728d366c6d0f764Af612cD47F3608E2B4d5B
Amounts
Core tracks balances in
base units
. During asset registration, the protocol records a
tickSize
for the Core asset, which specifies how many of the token's smallest units on L1 or Lighter EVM correspond to one Core
base unit
.
An asset's
tickSize
can be read from
L1InteropManager.getAssetConfig(assetIndex)
. If the asset is linked on EVM, EVM contracts can also read it from
EvmInteropManager.getAssetConfig(assetIndex)
. The two calls return:
Solidity
enum CanonicalDomain { None, L1, Core, EVM }

// L1InteropManager.getAssetConfig(uint32 assetIndex)
struct CoreAssetL1Config {
    CanonicalDomain canonicalDomain;
    address l1Token;
    address coreTokenAdmin;
    uint56 extensionMultiplier;
    uint128 tickSize;
    address l1Gateway;
}

// EvmInteropManager.getAssetConfig(uint32 assetIndex)
struct CoreAssetEvmConfig {
    CanonicalDomain canonicalDomain;
    address evmToken;
    address evmGateway;
    uint128 tickSize;
}
Convert from the token's smallest units to Core base units with
baseAmount = amount / tickSize
, and back with
amount = baseAmount * tickSize
.
As an example, ETH has
tickSize = 10^10
wei, so transferring 1 ETH (
10^18
wei) corresponds to
10^8
Core base units.
Routes
A route names the Core balance that a transfer uses:
Perps
for collateral in perpetuals markets, or
Spot
for the balance used in spot markets. Transfers involving Core specify a route. A transfer to Core credits the selected route, and a transfer from Core debits it.
New Core master accounts, including every account created through Lighter EVM, are
unified trading accounts
. A unified account keeps its USDC in one shared margin balance, so both routes credit and debit the same USDC. The
account-info read
reports this shared USDC collateral as
collateralBaseAmount
. It is not reserved exclusively for perpetuals and can also support spot operations, subject to margin requirements.
A USDC deposit through the
Spot
route can therefore leave the
spot-balance read
at zero while
collateralBaseAmount
increases. The spot read alone does not capture all funds usable for spot operations, and the shared collateral is not necessarily all available to spend.
Other assets enabled as margin for a unified account also prioritize the margin balance. Incoming amounts that exceed the remaining per-account or global supply cap stay in the separate spot balance. Enabling margin for an asset reallocates its existing spot balance in the same way, subject to those caps. USDC has no supply cap, and switching an account to unified mode moves all existing spot USDC into the margin balance.
The
Perps
route accepts an asset other than USDC only if the asset is enabled as margin for the account. ETH is currently not enabled as margin, so send ETH on the
Spot
route: an ETH deposit on the
Perps
route is
refunded
in full.
Core's
account API
reports an account's mode as
account_trading_mode
:
0
for classic,
1
for unified. A classic account keeps separate perps and spot balances.
The
RouteType
enum is ABI-encoded as
uint8
.
Solidity
enum RouteType {
    Perps, // 0
    Spot   // 1
}

EVM to Core
Any EVM address can send funds to a Core master account by calling
EvmInteropManager.sendToCore
. The
EvmInteropManager
takes the funds from the caller on EVM and submits a request for Core to credit the recipient account. Transfers to Core subaccounts are not supported.
The recipient master account is identified by its controlling address, which is either a Lighter EVM address or an Ethereum L1 address; see
Core accounts
. An EVM-controlled account is created on the first transfer if it does not exist yet. An L1-controlled account must already exist, otherwise the call reverts.
The first transfer to an EVM-controlled recipient requires an additional 146,000 gas to allocate account state on Core.
Submit a transfer
Solidity
function sendToCore(
    uint32 assetIndex,
    address to,
    bool isL1Account,
    uint256 amount,
    RouteType routeType
) external payable returns (uint64 reqId);
Type
Parameter
Description
uint32
assetIndex
Asset identifier.
address
to
Controlling address of the recipient Core master account.
bool
isL1Account
true
for an L1-controlled Core account;
false
for an EVM-controlled Core account.
uint256
amount
Amount in the token's smallest units on EVM, such as wei for ETH. Must be nonzero and a multiple of the asset's
tickSize
.
RouteType
routeType
Destination balance:
Perps = 0
or
Spot = 1
.
For an ERC-20, approve
EvmInteropManager
to spend
amount
of the configured EVM token. The contract pulls tokens from the caller.
Call
EvmInteropManager.sendToCore
. For ETH,
msg.value
must equal
amount
exactly. For an ERC-20,
msg.value
must be zero.
Keep the returned
reqId
to
check the transfer's status
once Core has processed it.
In examples below,
coreOwner
is the address controlling the recipient's Core master account. Set
isL1Account
to
true
for an L1-controlled account or
false
for an EVM-controlled account. Choose
routeType
as
RouteType.Perps
or
RouteType.Spot
to select the balance to credit.
After approving the manager, send ERC-20 tokens to the selected Core balance:
Solidity
uint64 reqId = EvmInteropManager.sendToCore(
    assetIndex,
    coreOwner,
    isL1Account,
    amount,
    routeType
);
For an ETH transfer to the same Core account and balance:
Solidity
uint64 reqId = EvmInteropManager.sendToCore{value: amount}(
    1,      // assetIndex: ETH
    coreOwner,
    isL1Account,
    amount,
    routeType
);
For tokens that support EIP-2612, use
sendToCoreWithPermit
to authorize spending and submit the transfer in one call. Pass the same parameters as
sendToCore
, followed by the permit's
deadline
,
v
,
r
, and
s
. The permit authorizes the manager to spend
amount
from the caller.
If the EVM call reverts, no assets move and no request is queued. A successful EVM transaction confirms that the request was submitted, but does not confirm how much Core credited.
Check transfer status
sendToCore
returns a
uint64 reqId
that identifies the request on Core. To check its outcome, look up
reqId
with the
transaction-status read
. Once Core has processed the request, the read returns
status == 1
. The response's
acceptedAmount
gives the amount credited in
Core base units
, which may be less than the requested amount or zero. See
Send to Core
for response decoding. Any unaccepted amount is refunded; see
Send to Core Refunds
.
Send to Core Refunds
For each
sendToCore
deposit, the Core sequencer determines how much to credit on Core. The
Send to Core response
reports this as
acceptedAmount
, expressed in
Core base units
, ranging from zero to
amount / tickSize
.
The sequencer currently enforces these rules:
It credits nothing when the asset is not registered on Core.
It credits nothing when the route is
Perps
and the asset is not enabled as margin for the recipient account; see
Routes
.
It credits less than the full amount, possibly nothing, when the deposit would take the account's balance of the asset past Core's maximum.
If the sequencer accepts less than the full
amount
, or none of it, Core refunds the difference. The refund amount, in units of the token's smallest denomination on EVM, is
amount - acceptedAmount * tickSize
. Refunds belong to the recipient
to
, even when a different address called
sendToCore
.
Core schedules the refund as a separate EVM transaction, so confirm its delivery separately from Core acceptance. Where it is delivered depends on the recipient's domain:
EVM-controlled recipient:
the refund goes to
to
on EVM. An ERC-20 refund passes through
EvmInteropManager
. An ETH refund is a plain value transfer to
to
.

Transfers between Ethereum L1 and Core move ETH or an asset with an active L1 representation. For an L1-native asset, this path becomes available after Core registration. For an EVM-native asset, its L1 wrapper must also be enabled. Core-native assets cannot be transferred to L1.
See
Token linking
for setup and
amounts
and
routes
for Core transfer conventions.
L1 to Core
Call
L1InteropManager.sendToCore(...)
on L1. The recipient is a Core master account identified by its controlling L1 address. If it does not exist, the deposit path allocates the account index and Core creates the account when processing the deposit.
Solidity
function sendToCore(
    uint32 assetIndex,
    address to,
    uint256 amount,
    RouteType routeType
) external payable;
amount
is in the L1 token's smallest units and must be a nonzero multiple of the asset's L1
tickSize
. Read the L1 configuration from
L1InteropManager.getAssetConfig(assetIndex)
. The deposit credits
amount / tickSize
Core base units
to the selected perps or spot route, subject to Core acceptance.
For an ERC-20, approve
L1InteropManager
to spend
amount
of the configured L1 token.
Call
sendToCore(...)
with the recipient's controlling L1 address. For ETH, use
assetIndex = 1
and send exactly
amount
as
msg.value
. For an ERC-20, send no ETH with the call.
Confirm the deposit's processing and credited amount in Core. A successful L1 receipt only confirms submission.
L1-native tokens are escrowed on L1. An EVM-native asset's L1 wrapper is burned through its selected mint gateway.
L1InteropManager
submits the deposit through
L1CoreMessaging
; applications do not call
registerDeposit(...)
directly.
This deposit path targets L1-controlled masters, not subaccounts or EVM-controlled masters. Use a supported internal Core transfer to move funds into a subaccount after depositing.
Unaccepted deposits
If Core does not accept the full deposit, the unaccepted amount is returned to the original deposit destination through a Core-originated
L1 Call
. It belongs to
to
, which may differ from the address that paid for the deposit. Follow
Core message execution on L1
to complete delivery once the call is ready.
Core to L1
Initiating a Core withdrawal
A withdrawal to L1 can be initiated in three ways, depending on the account's controller.
From Core.
Submit one of the following
signed transactions
.
Withdraw (
txType = 13
).
L1-controlled Core accounts can withdraw to their controlling L1 address using only an API-key signature. No controller ECDSA signature is required.
Withdraw to L1 Address (
txType = 132
).
L1-controlled or EVM-controlled Core accounts can specify an L1 recipient. This requires both an API-key signature and the EOA controller's ECDSA signature, even when withdrawing to the controller's own address.
From L1.
The controlling L1 address calls
L1CoreMessaging.withdraw(...)
to withdraw to itself, or
L1CoreMessaging.withdrawToL1Address(...)
to specify a recipient.
From EVM.
The controlling EVM address calls
EvmToCoreEntrypoint.withdrawToL1Address(...)
.
A contract controller cannot supply an ECDSA signature and must use its native-domain call for the explicit-recipient option. The debit account may be the controller's master account or one of its subaccounts, subject to Core authorization.
Finalizing a Core withdrawal
Once Core accepts the withdrawal and its batch has been
executed on L1
, follow
Executing Core messages on L1
to retrieve the call data and execute the call.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.title: L1 and EVM
Introduction
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-int.content:
Lighter EVM is an EVM-equivalent rollup designed for native interoperability with Lighter Core. It enables general-purpose applications to compose directly with Lighter Core markets and liquidity at low latency while preserving the verifiable security guarantees users expect from the Lighter ecosystem.
Devnet
The current devnet runs the full protocol stack with interop enabled:
Lighter EVM
is the EVM-equivalent execution environment where you deploy and interact with smart contracts.
Lighter Core
is the order matching engine. EVM contracts can read and write to Core, and Core accounts can send assets to Lighter EVM. See
Lighter Interop
.
A privately deployed L1
stands in for Ethereum as the settlement and data availability layer. See
L1 and EVM token transfers
for moving assets between L1 and Lighter EVM.
Chain parameters and contract addresses are listed in
Chain Info
.
📘
Limitations
The devnet version uses mocked ZK proofs for L1 finalization.
The permissionless
escape hatch
is not fully functional on the devnet.
RPC calls that
read Core
only work at the
latest
block. Support for earlier blocks is planned for an upcoming update.
Next steps
Getting Started
walks through sending your first transaction on Lighter EVM.
Technical Architecture
explains how L1, Lighter EVM, and Lighter Core fit together.
Differences from L1 EVM
lists the behaviors of Lighter EVM that differ from Ethereum.
Lighter Interop
covers reading Core from EVM, writing to Core, and moving assets between the two.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-l1-.title: L1 Data Fee
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-l1-.content:
Lighter EVM publishes
pubdata
— the data required to reconstruct public protocol state — to L1 Ethereum blobs. Pubdata currently consists of state diffs and EVM-to-Core write responses. In addition to the ordinary execution fee, every fee-paying transaction pays an
L1 data fee
(also called the
pubdata fee
) for its metered pubdata contribution.
The data fee has two independent inputs:
The transaction's pubdata contribution
, metered deterministically during execution.
The price per pubdata byte
, published by the sequencer once per block.
These inputs estimate the transaction's share of the eventual L1 data-availability cost.
Note that state-diff contributions to pubdata are metered per block, even though the state-diff submitted to L1 is aggregated across many blocks. This is done so the sequencer can issue pre-confirmations without knowing the eventual batch boundary.
Since this necessarily over-estimates the actual byte-contribution, the sequencer accounts for this expected aggregation when selecting the trusted
blobBaseFee
, amortizing the expected batch blob cost over the block-metered bytes.
Pubdata contribution
A transaction's metered pubdata contribution has two parts:
state diffs
and
EVM-to-Core write responses
.
State diffs
When a transaction changes an account, the protocol meters differences in four account-state components:
nonce
,
balance
,
code
, and
storage
. Each component materialized in the evolving block diff contributes its encoded size:
Account field
Bytes
Nonce
32
Balance
32
Storage slot
64 (32-byte key + 32-byte value)
Code
Length of the runtime code
Two structural overheads are charged alongside the fields: a 25-byte header for each account that appears in the diff, and a one-time 4-byte length prefix for each account with storage entries.
Metering uses the state at the beginning of the block as its baseline:
Divergence materializes a field.
A field is added to the evolving diff when it first differs from its pre-block value.
The first writer pays while the field remains materialized.
Later transactions can overwrite an already-materialized field without adding pubdata bytes.
Restoration removes a field.
Returning a field to its pre-block value removes its bytes from the evolving diff. The resulting refund is applied at settlement and does not replenish the transaction's in-flight budget.
Clearing storage is not inherently free.
Setting an old non-zero slot to zero still differs from its pre-block value and is therefore a charged write. Only restoration to the pre-block value removes the entry.
Self-destruct removes only same-transaction creations.
Under current EVM semantics, self-destruct deletes an account only when it was created in the same transaction. Deletion removes the bytes materialized for the account's nonce, code, and storage. Note that if the address held funds before the block, account-clearing implies the state of the account's balance goes from non-zero to zero, which is charged for.
EVM-to-Core write responses
Each EVM-to-Core write is charged for a response record consisting of a 1-byte status header plus the greater of the success and error payload widths for its write type. The resulting charge is 1–9 bytes.
Price per byte
The sequencer publishes
blobBaseFee
once per block; the
GasPriceOracle
predeploy at
0x660000000000000000000000000000000000000d
exposes the current value. The protocol derives the price per pubdata byte as:
Text
pricePerPubdataByte = ceil(blobBaseFee * GAS_PER_BLOB / BYTES_PER_BLOB)
                    = ceil(blobBaseFee * 131072 / 126976)
131072
is the EIP-4844 gas per blob and
126976
is the usable pubdata capacity of a blob.
blobBaseFee
is a trusted sequencer input: the protocol uses the published value and does not verify it against L1.
Transaction lifecycle
The pubdata-charging lifecycle has four phases:
Validation.
The protocol computes a deterministic intrinsic byte reservation and rejects the transaction if the reservation does not fit its pubdata budget or the block's remaining pubdata capacity.
Pre-execution.
A fee-paying transaction prepays its maximum possible data fee.
Execution.
State-diff growth and EVM-to-Core responses consume the transaction's pubdata budget.
Settlement.
The final fee is credited to the pubdata fee vault and the unused reserve is returned to the sender.
Validation
Each transaction has a hard pubdata byte limit derived from its gas limit:
Text
pubdataByteLimit = floor(gasLimit / PUBDATA_GAS_PER_BYTE)
PUBDATA_GAS_PER_BYTE = 70
Pubdata accounting is independent of execution gas: the
GAS
opcode is unaffected, but
gasLimit
controls both the execution-gas limit and the pubdata byte limit.
For an ordinary fee-paying transaction, the intrinsic reservation is:
Text
intrinsicPubdataBytes = 260 + 80 * authorizationListLength
The fixed
260
bytes cover the sender's account header, balance, and nonce together with the account headers and balances of the three fee vaults. Each EIP-7702 authorization tuple adds a conservative
80
bytes for an account header, nonce, and delegation designation. Fee-exempt exogenous transactions cannot carry an authorization list and reserve
89
intrinsic bytes for the sender's account header, balance, and nonce.
The transaction is rejected before execution if
intrinsicPubdataBytes
exceeds
pubdataByteLimit
, or if it does not fit into the block's remaining pubdata capacity (see
Block limit
). The reservation itself is deducted from the pubdata budget when execution starts.
Pre-execution
Before an ordinary transaction executes, the sender prepays its maximum possible data fee:
Text
maxPubdataFee = pubdataByteLimit * pricePerPubdataByte
Increasing
gasLimit
therefore requires a larger up-front balance, but unused execution gas and unused pubdata reserve are returned at settlement.
Execution
The execution budget begins at
pubdataByteLimit - intrinsicPubdataBytes
. State-diff growth and EVM-to-Core response records consume this budget. State-diff removals reduce the final charge but do not restore budget during execution.
If a message call or contract creation exceeds the remaining pubdata budget, that frame reverts to its checkpoint, and the pubdata consumed within the frame is returned to the execution budget. This is not an exceptional halt, so unused gas is also refunded. The transaction reverts only if the failure propagates to the top level.
Settlement
At settlement, the metered contribution is:
Text
stateDiffBytes = max(0, intrinsicPubdataBytes + addedStateDiffBytes - removedStateDiffBytes)
meteredPubdataBytes = stateDiffBytes + interopResponseBytes
l1Fee = meteredPubdataBytes * pricePerPubdataByte
Fee-exempt exogenous transactions follow the same byte metering and budget rules but do not prepay or settle an L1 data fee inside the EVM.
Block limit
The cumulative metered contribution of a block may not exceed
MAX_EVM_PUBDATA_BYTES_PER_BLOCK = 253,952
bytes, the usable capacity of two blobs. A transaction is rejected at
validation
if its intrinsic reservation alone does not fit. Runtime consumption that would cross the limit triggers the same frame-revert behavior as exhausting the transaction's own budget.
Fee vaults
Transaction fees are routed to three predeploy vaults:
Fee component
Destination
Base fee
BaseFeeVault
(
0x660000000000000000000000000000000000000a
)
L1 data fee
PubdataFeeVault
(
0x660000000000000000000000000000000000000b
)
Priority tip
SequencerFeeVault
(
0x6600000000000000000000000000000000000002
)
COINBASE
returns the
SequencerFeeVault
address. Unlike L1 Ethereum, Lighter EVM does not burn base fees; it sends them to the
BaseFeeVault
.
Receipt fields
eth_getTransactionReceipt
exposes the metered data fee through three fields:
Receipt field
Meaning
l1GasUsed
Pubdata bytes metered for the transaction
l1GasPrice
Price per pubdata byte, in wei
l1Fee
l1GasUsed × l1GasPrice
, in wei
Fee-exempt exogenous transactions still report their metered bytes in
l1GasUsed
, but report
l1GasPrice = 0
and
l1Fee = 0
. See the
JSON-RPC API
for details. The standard
gasUsed
and
effectiveGasPrice
fields continue to report execution-gas accounting separately.
Impacts on account abstraction (ERC-4337)
Lighter EVM provides ERC-4337
EntryPoint
versions 0.6 through 0.9 as
preinstalls
.
The L1 data fee is charged to the sender of the outer L2 transaction. For an ERC-4337 bundle, that sender is the bundler's EOA. The
EntryPoint
meters and reimburses execution gas, but it does not measure Lighter EVM pubdata or reimburse the bundler for the resulting data fee.
Bundlers can recover this cost by adding a data-fee margin to each
UserOperation
's
preVerificationGas
, the ERC-4337 field for per-operation overhead that is not measured directly by
EntryPoint
execution.
Pricing a UserOperation
For the safest one-operation-per-transaction policy described
below
, price the full pubdata budget of the outer L2 transaction:
Text
pubdataByteLimit = floor(transactionGasLimit / PUBDATA_GAS_PER_BYTE)
dataFeeWei = pubdataByteLimit * pricePerPubdataByte

estimatedUserOpGasPrice =
  min(maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas + estimatedBlockBaseFee)

dataFeeGas = ceil(dataFeeWei / estimatedUserOpGasPrice)
transactionGasLimit
is the outer L2 transaction's gas limit, not an individual
UserOperation
gas-limit field.
pricePerPubdataByte
is calculated from the current
blobBaseFee
as described
above
.
Add
dataFeeGas
to
preVerificationGas
. Because
blobBaseFee
and the block base fee may change before inclusion, bundlers should add padding and round up. Apply any safety margin on
estimatedUserOpGasPrice
downward: a lower denominator produces a larger, more conservative
dataFeeGas
.
This calculation deliberately uses the transaction's worst-case pubdata budget. It will overcharge operations that materialize less pubdata, but it prevents the bundler from under-recovering the transaction-level fee.
Bundling policy
The protocol enforces one pubdata budget for the outer L2 transaction, not a separate budget for each
UserOperation
. A multi-operation bundle therefore has no enforceable per-operation allocation. A successful operation can consume more of the shared budget than the bundler expected, leaving later operations without enough pubdata budget and potentially causing them to fail.
Sending one
UserOperation
per L2 transaction aligns the priced operation with the protocol-enforced budget. This trades bundling efficiency for predictable fee recovery and removes cross-operation pubdata interference.
Smart contract guidance
Pack values into fewer storage slots and reuse already-materialized slots where practical.
Do not treat clearing a storage slot as a pubdata optimization. It saves pubdata only when it restores the slot's pre-block value.
Increase
gasLimit
when pubdata is the binding resource. This increases the pubdata budget as well as the execution-gas limit.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-tec.title: Technical Architecture
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/evm-tec.content:
Lighter EVM is an EVM-equivalent execution environment that runs as a sidecar to Lighter Core, the high-performance order matching engine at the heart of the Lighter protocol. Together, they form a unified rollup that settles on Ethereum L1 with zero-knowledge proofs.
This page provides a high-level overview of the system architecture and how its components fit together. For detailed specifications, see the linked pages throughout.
Design principles
The architecture is built around four goals:
Non-custodial execution.
Users retain full control of their assets at all times. The protocol enforces this through on-chain escrow, deterministic bridging, and an escape hatch mechanism that allows withdrawals even if the sequencer goes offline.
Verifiable state transitions.
Every state update, across both EVM and Core, is proven with zero-knowledge proofs before being accepted on L1. No trusted operator can forge state.
Native interoperability.
EVM smart contracts can read Core state synchronously and write to Core asynchronously, enabling DeFi applications to compose directly with Lighter's order book liquidity.
Scalability.
The dual-execution model separates general-purpose smart contract execution from the optimized order matching engine, allowing each to scale independently.
System overview
The system spans three domains that interoperate through a shared protocol:
Ethereum (L1)
serves as the settlement and data availability layer. The L1 bridge contract verifies ZK proofs and finalizes batches, and L1 smart contracts manage the priority queue and token escrow for cross-chain operations.
Lighter EVM
is an EVM-equivalent chain that executes general-purpose smart contracts. It supports standard Ethereum transaction types and exposes a system precompile for synchronous reads into Core state.
Lighter Core
is the specialized execution engine that handles order matching, account management, and derivatives trading with low latency.
Key components
Sequencer
The sequencer orchestrates both execution environments. It ingests transactions from separate Core and EVM mempools, maintains the write streams, pairs EVM blocks with Core blocks, and periodically bundles state diffs into batches for L1 submission.
Witness node
The witness node ingests data from L1 and re-executes both Core and EVM transactions to materialize the execution traces needed for proving. It serves as the data pipeline between the sequencer and the prover.
Prover
The prover generates ZK proofs that verify every state transition in the protocol. It contains three classes of circuits:
EVM circuits
are OpenVM programs that verify the EVM state transition function, including reads from Core and write stream updates.
Core circuits
verify the Core state transition function, including write fulfillment.
Aggregation circuits
are OpenVM programs that combine the EVM and Core proofs into a single batch proof submitted to L1.
Smart contracts
Smart contracts on both L1 and EVM enforce the protocol rules. On L1, the bridge contract accepts batch commitments, verifies ZK proofs, and finalizes state. Additional L1 contracts manage the priority queue, cross-domain asset registration, and token escrow. On the EVM side, a set of predeploy contracts provide the entry points for interop writes, withdrawals, L1 message relay, and fee collection.
Rollup state
The protocol maintains a unified global state across both execution environments:
Component
Description
EVM state
EVM state stored as a Merkle Patricia Trie — accounts, storage, code.
Core state
Lighter Core state tree — accounts, orders, positions, balances.
EVM write stream
Ring buffer of pending Core-to-EVM async write requests.
Core write stream
Ring buffer of pending EVM-to-Core async write requests.
Each EVM block is paired with exactly one Core block, called its
parent Core block
. This pairing establishes a causal ordering: the EVM block has synchronous read access to the Core block's post-state, and re-orgs in Core automatically propagate to dependent EVM blocks.
Native EVM and Core Interoperability
EVM and Core communicate through two complementary channels.
Synchronous reads from EVM to Core
A system precompile allows EVM smart contracts to query Core state within a single transaction. Supported queries include account info, balances, positions, and market metadata. Since reads target the pinned Core block's state, they are deterministic and require no cross-chain messaging.
Asynchronous writes
State-modifying operations between domains flow through
write streams
.
EVM to Core:
An EVM transaction calls the
EvmToCoreEntrypoint
or
EvmInteropManager
predeploy, which appends a request to the Core write stream. The Core sequencer picks up the request and fulfills it in a subsequent Core block. Supported operations include canceling orders and sending tokens to Core.
Core to EVM:
A Core transaction enqueues a write to the EVM write stream. The EVM sequencer derives an exogenous transaction to fulfill it, minting or transferring tokens on the EVM side.
This design decouples execution, neither chain blocks on the other, while maintaining protocol-level safety through the write stream commitments verified in the ZK proofs.
Batch lifecycle and finalization
The protocol periodically groups Core and EVM state changes, including cross-domain writes, into
batches
. The associated diffs are published in blobs, and their commitments are recorded on L1. Each batch then advances through three ordered stages.
Commit.
The batch metadata and blob commitments are submitted to the L1 bridge. This records the proposed batch on L1
without
proving that it is correct.
Verify.
A zero-knowledge proof establishes the correctness of the committed batch, asserting the committed state roots and DA represent the outcomes of a valid state transition.
Execute.
The bridge finalizes the verified batch and advances the canonical state. Withdrawals (from either Core or EVM) included in the batch become claimable on L1.
Governance can revert a committed or verified batch until it is executed. An executed batch cannot be reverted.
Token bridging
Assets can move freely between L1, EVM, and Core. Each token has exactly one
canonical domain
where the real token lives. On other domains, a 1:1 wrapped representation is minted, backed by tokens locked in an escrow contract on the canonical chain.
Escape hatch
If the sequencer or prover becomes unavailable, the protocol includes a permissionless escape mechanism named desert mode. Anyone can activate it once a priority request or a pending cross-domain write remains unfulfilled past a timeout. From that point on:
Core freezes.
L1-controlled Core accounts exit their balances directly on L1 by submitting ZK proofs of their balances against the frozen Core state commitment.
EVM keeps running.
Users continue to force-include transactions through the L1 priority queue, and proving becomes fully permissionless: anyone can advance the chain by submitting a proof for one batch at a time. This lets users unwind DeFi positions and surface withdrawable balances. EVM-controlled Core accounts can still move their balances to EVM.
This ensures that users can always recover their assets, regardless of operator liveness.
