https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/get-sta.title: Get Started
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/get-sta.content:
Welcome to the Lighter SDK and API Introduction. Here, we will go through everything from the system setup, to creating and cancelling all types of orders, to fetching exchange data.
To keep up to date with Lighter's API, join this
Telegram Channel
or #api-updates on our
Discord
. System upgrades are also announced there (#system-upgrades on Discord), and can be monitored programmatically via
https://status.lighter.xyz/
.
This page uses the Python SDK. Using TypeScript? See
Quickstart: TypeScript + WASM
. Base URLs, chain IDs, testnet and colocation are listed in
Environments & endpoints
, and Robinhood Chain in
Lighter on Robinhood Chain
.
The full API reference is available at
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/reference
. You can also download the OpenAPI specs directly:
Main API (
https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/
):
page.json
Explorer API (
https://explorer.elliot.ai/api
):
explorer endpoints.json
Install the SDK
Python:
Shell
pip install lighter-sdk
Go:
Shell
go get https://github.com/elliottech/lighter-go
Find Your Account Index
Your account index is Lighter's integer identifier for your account. If you use sub-accounts, there will be multiple account indexes tied to the same L1 wallet. Query it using your L1 (Ethereum) address:
Python
import asyncio
import lighter

BASE_URL = "https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai"
L1_ADDRESS = "0x123"

async def main():
    client = lighter.ApiClient(lighter.Configuration(host=BASE_URL))
    resp = await lighter.AccountApi(client).accounts_by_l1_address(l1_address=L1_ADDRESS)
    print(resp.sub_accounts[0].index)
    await client.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
Create an API Key
API keys enable SDK signing and authenticated API requests; each is tied to a single account index and has its own nonce. You can use indices 4-254. Indices 0-3 are reserved for the web/mobile interfaces. Finally, the 255 index can be used as a value for the
api_key_index
parameter of the
apikeys
method of the
AccountApi
for getting the data about all the API keys. See this page for
more details
.
Initialize the Signer Client
In order to create a transaction (create/cancel/modify order), you need to use the SignerClient. Initialize with the following code:
Python
client = lighter.SignerClient(  
        url=BASE_URL,  
        api_private_keys={API_KEY_INDEX:PRIVATE_KEY},  
        account_index=ACCOUNT_INDEX
    )
The code for the signer can be found in the same repo, in the
signer_client.py
file. You may notice that it uses a binary for the signer: the code for it can be found in the
lighter-go
public repo, and you can compile it yourself using the
justfile
.
Nonce
When signing a transaction, you may need to provide a nonce (number used once). A nonce needs to be incremented each time you sign something. You can get the next nonce that you need to use using the
TransactionApi’s
next_nonce
method or take care of incrementing it yourself. Note that each nonce is handled per
API_KEY
. Skipping nonces, and which rejected transactions consume a nonce, are covered in
Core concepts
.
Signing a transaction
One can sign a transaction using the
SignerClient’s
sign_create_order
,
sign_modify_order
,
sign_cancel_order
and its other similar methods. For actually pushing the transaction, you need to call
send_tx
or
send_tx_batch
using the
TransactionApi
. Here’s an
example
that includes such an operation. Alternatively, you can use
create_order
, which will send the tx as well. See more details
here
.
Note that
base_amount, price
are to be passed as integers, and
client_order_index
is a unique (across all markets) identifier you provide for you to be able to reference this order later (e.g. if you want to cancel it). The SDK handles nonce management automatically. For complex systems, you can implement local nonce management.
Price and Size precision
Query the
orderBookDetails
endpoint to get decimal precision for each market (see
Integer prices and sizes
):
Shell
GET /api/v1/orderBookDetails
Place Your First Market Order
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.create_order(
        market_index=0, # ETH perps market
        client_order_index=1234, 
        base_amount=10,  # 0.001 ETH
        price=3100_00,  # $3100 -- worst acceptable price for the order
        is_ask=False, # Bid, i.e. buy order
        order_type=client.ORDER_TYPE_MARKET,
        time_in_force=client.ORDER_TIME_IN_FORCE_IMMEDIATE_OR_CANCEL,
        reduce_only=False,
        order_expiry=client.DEFAULT_IOC_EXPIRY,
    )
Place Your First Limit Order
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.create_order(
        market_index=0, # ETH perps market
        client_order_index=1234,
        base_amount=100,  # 0.01 ETH
        price=2900_00,  # $2900
        is_ask=False,  # Bid, i.e. buy order
        order_type=client.ORDER_TYPE_LIMIT,
        time_in_force=client.ORDER_TIME_IN_FORCE_GOOD_TILL_TIME,
        reduce_only=False,
        order_expiry=client.DEFAULT_28_DAY_ORDER_EXPIRY,
    )
Cancel an order
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.cancel_order(
        market_index=market_index,
        order_index=1234
    )
Modify an order
Python
tx, tx_hash, err = await client.modify_order(
        market_index=0,
        order_index=1234,
        base_amount=100,  # 0.01 ETH
        price=2800_00,  # $2800
    )
Authentication Tokens
For REST API calls and Websocket channels requiring authentication:
Python
auth_token, err = client.create_auth_token_with_expiry(
            deadline=3600, # seconds. Max is 8 hours, default is 10 minutes
            api_key_index=API_KEY_INDEX,
        )
Alternatively, you can use a read-only auth token. See more details
here
.
API via SDK
The SDK provides API classes that make calling the Lighter API easier. Here are some of them and the most important of their methods:
AccountApi
- provides account data
account
- get account data either by l1_address or index
accounts_by_l1_address
- get data about all the accounts (master account and subaccounts)
apikeys
- get data about the api keys of an account (use api_key_index = 255 for getting data about all the api keys)
TransactionApi
- provides transaction-related data
next_nonce
- get next nonce to be used for signing a transaction using a certain api key
send_tx
- push a transaction
send_tx_batch
- push several transactions at once
OrderApi
- provides data about orders, trades and the orderbook
order_book_details
- get data about a specific market’s orderbook
order_books
- get data about all markets’ orderbooks
You can find the rest
here
. We also provide an
example
showing how to use some of these. For the methods that require an auth token, you can generate one using the
create_auth_token_with_expiry
method of the
SignerClient
(the same applies to the websockets auth).
WebSockets
Lighter also provides access to essential info using websockets. A simple version of an
WsClient
for subscribing to account and orderbook updates is implemented
here
. You can also take it as an example implementation of such a client.
To get access to more data, you will need to connect to the websockets without the provided WsClient. You can find the streams you can connect to, how to connect, and the data they provide in the
websockets
section.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/histori.title: Historical Data
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/histori.content:
Users can fetch historical data using various REST endpoints, mainly:
accountInactiveOrders
trades
logs
tx
pnl
deposit_history
,
transfer_history
,
withdraw_history
candles
fundings
,
positionFunding
liquidations
exchangeMetrics
,
executeStats
Several of these are heavy (see the weights in
Rate Limits
), so paginate and cache the results.
Alternatively, you can use
export
to obtain CSVs containing up to 12 months of trades, or up to 3 months of funding payments, for a specific account index.
Historical Trade Events
For interested parties, you can access parquet files containing trade events (global), up to mainnet genesis (January 17th, 2025), using the
historicalTrade
endpoint. To obtain access, perform an in-app transfer of 100 LIT to
0x4FD058F25bE85E459ec552cA8e4C696FD1D34125
. On-chain transfers are not supported; you must transfer from within the exchange directly (
L2Transfer
).
Historical Trade Events (Requester Pays)
For those that prefer to use their AWS account, and cover costs per each request themselves,
--request-payer requester
can be used.
Example request for Lighter Core:
Shell
aws s3 ls s3://lighter-historical-data/trade-daily/ --request-payer requester | tail -3
aws s3 cp s3://lighter-historical-data/trade-daily/date=2025-11-26/trades.parquet /tmp/trades.parquet --request-payer requester
Hourly Open Interest (Requester Pays)
Hourly open interest for every perps market is published to the same bucket under
open-interest-hourly/
, as one Parquet file per UTC day. Each row is the end-of-hour snapshot of one market:
Column
Type
Description
hour
timestamp (UTC)
Start of the hour
symbol
string
Market symbol, e.g.
BTC
open_interest
double
Open interest in the base asset
mark_price
double
Mark price at the snapshot
open_interest_usd
double
open_interest * mark_price
Data starts at mainnet genesis (January 17th, 2025) and a new day is added every night.
Example request for Lighter Core:
Shell
aws s3 ls s3://lighter-historical-data/open-interest-hourly/ --request-payer requester | tail -3
aws s3 cp s3://lighter-historical-data/open-interest-hourly/date=2026-10-15/oi.parquet /tmp/oi.parquet --request-payer requester

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/manage-.title: Manage Public Pools
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/manage-.content:
Something to keep in mind is that Lighter considers Public Pools as a special type of Subaccount, where multiple users in addition to its owner can deposit in exchange for pool shares. You can create up to 6 public pools per L1 address. Creation is gated to having traded $10M or more in paid volume (checked hourly). You can trade on it via API as you would with a subaccount: users can participate in Public Pools by creating and modifying them, but also mint and burn shares via API. The corresponding transaction types are:
TxTypeL2CreatePublicPool (10)
TxTypeL2UpdatePublic Pool (11)
TxL2TypeMintShares (18)
TxL2TypeBurnShares (19)
In the hyperlinks, you can find the corresponding examples on the Python SDK using wrapper functions.
You can monitor your shares using the
account
endpoint, the
publicPoolsMetadata
endpoint, or any Websocket channel that contains the
PoolShares JSON
. Note that
entry_usdc
represents the USDC used to acquire pool shares - if you're looking to get an accurate price per share to date, you can query the
publicPoolsMetadata
endpoint using
account_id
plus one. Staking pools are to be considered similar to public pools in structure, wth
principal_amount
representing the number of coins staked.
This is what a request to fetch LLP's (281474976710654) metadata would look like:
Shell
curl --request GET \
     --url 'https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/publicPoolsMetadata?index=281474976710655&limit=1' \
     --header 'accept: application/json'

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/partner.title: Partner Attribution
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/partner.content:
This guide explains how partners can integrate with Lighter programmatically to earn additional fees for trades executed through their applications, or just for tracking purposes. The program is permissionless, allowing any account index to be used to collect fees, including subaccounts.
Definitions
Partner
: You, the integrator building on top of Lighter.
Client
: Your user, or customer, whose transactions you send on their behalf. Both Standard and Premium/Advanced accounts are accepted.
Requirements
Trades containing partner attribution attributes with non-zero integrator fees will require the client submitting them to be on a Plus or Premium/Advanced
account type
. To check the account type of a client, you can use the
accountLimits
endpoint. To change account type, use
changeAccountTier
. Zero-fee attribution (tracking only) works on any account type, including Standard.
Integrator Approval
Before you can append partner attributes to client transactions, they must submit a
ApproveIntegrator
transaction. Approving an account index associated with a different L1 address requires an L1 signature. However, if the account index is associated with the same L1 address, or fees are zero, only an L2 signature is needed.  This transaction authorizes you to charge additional taker/maker fees on trades originating from orders created through your platform, as defined via the
systemConfig
endpoint.
Binary options use the client's
spot
approval limits (
max_spot_taker_fee
,
max_spot_maker_fee
) and the system-wide spot caps. Their integrator fees are scaled by the trade price; see
Binary options: Partner attribution
.
At any point in time, there can only be a maximum of 4 approved Partners per Client.
Example
Python: signature
client.approve_integrator(
        eth_private_key=STRING,
        integrator_account_index=INTEGER,
        max_perps_taker_fee=INTEGER,
        max_perps_maker_fee=INTEGER,
        max_spot_taker_fee=INTEGER,
        max_spot_maker_fee=INTEGER,
        approval_expiry=INTEGER # in ms  
    )
Python: example
client.approve_integrator(
        eth_private_key="",
        integrator_account_index=1234,
        max_perps_taker_fee=1000, # 10 bps
        max_perps_maker_fee=1000, # 10 bps
        max_spot_taker_fee=1000,  # 10 bps
        max_spot_maker_fee=1000,  # 10 bps
        approval_expiry=1775518466000 # in ms
    )
TypeScript (WASM)
const tx = check(lighter.SignApproveIntegrator(
  PARTNER_ACCOUNT_INDEX,
  1000,   // maxPerpsTakerFee  (1000 = 10 bps)
  1000,   // maxPerpsMakerFee
  1000,   // maxSpotTakerFee
  1000,   // maxSpotMakerFee
  Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 3600e3, // approvalExpiry, unix ms
  0, await nextNonce(), API_KEY_INDEX, CLIENT_ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));

// If the partner account belongs to a different L1 address and fees > 0,
// the client's wallet must sign tx.messageToSign → txInfo.L1Sig
You can find the full Python example
here
. The TypeScript example uses the WASM signer from the
TypeScript quickstart
; see
When an L1 signature is required
. To revoke an integrator before the allowance expires, you can send another
ApproveIntegrator
request setting all fees to zero, requiring just an L2 signature.
Fields Explanation
IntegratorAccountIndex
: Partner's account index. All partner fees collected from client trades will be credited to this account. For perpetual markets, the fees are paid and credited in USDC (perps). For spot markets, the fees are paid and credited in the received asset (e.g. buying spot ETH means the Client pays fees in ETH directly).
Max Fees
: These values define the maximum fees you are allowed to charge your client.
Fees are calculated as:
fee(bps) = trade_size × (fee_value / 1e6)
Example:
MaxPerpsTakerFee = 500
500 / 1e6 = 0.0005 = 5 basis points
This means you can charge up to
5 bps
of the trade quote for each perpetual taker order.
System-wide Maximums
Lighter enforces global maximum fee limits. If you submit an approval transaction exceeding these limits, the transaction will fail. Current limits can be checked via the
systemConfig
endpoint.
ApprovalExpiry
The timestamp when the integrator approval expires in a form of Unix timestamp in
milliseconds
. After this time, the partner must obtain approval again from the client.
The maximum value you can send is equivalent to
2^48-1
.
Creating Orders for Your Client
Once the integrator approval is successfully submitted, you can begin sending transactions for the client and collecting partner fees.
When creating orders, include the following fields:
Python
IntegratorAccountIndex: INTEGER # the partner account index, where integrator fees will accrue
IntegratorMakerFee: INTEGER     # fee the partner wants to charge for maker trades
IntegratorTakerFee: INTEGER     # fee the partner wants to charge for taker trades
These fees
must not exceed the maximum values
defined during the approval step. The same fields exist on modify and grouped orders.
🚧
Non-zero partner fees can't be combined with custom self-trade prevention
If an order sets a non-zero
integratorTakerFee
or
integratorMakerFee
together with any self-trade mode other than the default (
0, 0
: expire maker, same account index), it is rejected with
21159
"self-trade specifications are not allowed when there are non-zero fees". Zero-fee attribution (tracking only) works with any self-trade mode.
Example: Creating an Order
Python
client.create_order(
        market_index=0,
        client_order_index=0, # bound to 2^48-1
        base_amount=1000,  # decimals as described in the orderBookDetails endpoint
        price=4050_00,  # decimals as described in the orderBookDetails endpoint
        is_ask=True, # sell
        order_type=client.ORDER_TYPE_LIMIT,
        time_in_force=client.ORDER_TIME_IN_FORCE_GOOD_TILL_TIME,
        reduce_only=False,
        trigger_price=0,
        integrator_account_index=integrator_account_index,
        integrator_taker_fee=integrator_taker_fee,
        integrator_maker_fee=integrator_maker_fee,
        nonce=nonce,
        api_key_index=api_key_index,
    )
TypeScript (WASM)
lighter.SignCreateOrder(
  marketIndex, clientOrderIndex, baseAmount, price, isAsk, orderType, tif,
  reduceOnly, triggerPrice, orderExpiry,
  PARTNER_ACCOUNT_INDEX, // integratorAccountIndex
  500,                   // integratorTakerFee (5 bps) – must be ≤ approved max
  200,                   // integratorMakerFee (2 bps)
  0, 0, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, CLIENT_ACCOUNT_INDEX,
);
You can find the full Python example
here
.
Design tips
Show your fee clearly in the order ticket.
Request an approval expiry that matches your product (e.g. 1 year) and re-prompt before it lapses.
Use a dedicated sub-account as your integrator account to keep revenue separate.
Track attributed volume and fees with
partnerStats
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/priorit.title: Priority Transactions
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/priorit.content:
Priority Transactions offer a way to interact with the Lighter protocol directly via Ethereum directly. You can think of them as censorship-resistant operations - and use them to e.g. cancel all orders or withdraw your collateral. They can be executed via Lighter's proxy smart contract on Ethereum, which holds the platform's collateral:
0x3B4D794a66304F130a4Db8F2551B0070dfCf5ca7
. Everything here works even if Lighter's API is unavailable.
Read functions
:
addressToAccountIndex
: the master account index of a layer 1 address.
desertMode
: boolean, set to False unless desert mode gets activated.
getPendingBalance
: the pending balance for a certain layer 1 account, you can find a complete list of asset IDs via the assetDetails
endpoint
.
getPendingBalanceLegacy
: the pending balance for a certain layer 1 account before the spot upgrade. In this case, it can only be a USDC value.
lastAccountIndex
: the highest account index assigned. Only accounts that deposit get assigned an account index, so that would represent the total number of wallets on the exchange.
tokenToAssetIndex
: match an ERC20 contract address to its corresponding asset_index on the Lighter protocol
Most have been left out, but you can check out all functions on Ethereum block explorers, e.g.
Etherscan
.
Write functions
:
activateDesertMode
burnShares
: allows you to burn shares of a Public Pool.
cancelAllorders
: cancels all open orders on Lighter for the specified account index.
cancelOustandingDepositsForDesertMode
changePubKey
: assign a newly created api key to an account index. Each key is tied to a single account index (if you use sub-accounts, you'll need to create new ones).
createOrder
: submit reduce-only IOC orders
deposit
: deposit assets to the platform. See
Deposits, Transfers and Withdrawals
for more details.
depositBatch
: deposit to multiple addresses.
transferERC20
: transfer non-ETH spot assets between addresses.
transferETH
: transfer mainnet ETH between addresses.
withdraw
: withdraw assets from the platform. See
Deposits, Transfers and Withdrawals
for more details.
withdrawPendingBalance
: claim an existing secure withdrawal. Whenever the gas isn't too steep in price, withdrawals will be claimed by the platform on the users' behalf.
withdrawPendingBalanceLegacy
: claim an existing secure withdrawal that was requested before the addition of spot assets to the protocol.
Unlisted functions are reserved for the governor (a multi-sig controlled by the protocol) to manage markets and the protocol's settings. If you specify an account_index, you should sign with the wallet that controls said index.
Audits and the vulnerability disclosure policy:
docs.lighter.xyz/security
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/rate-li.content:
We enforce rate limits on both REST API and WebSocket usage. These limits apply to both IP address and L1 address. It's important to note that for non-standard account types, sendTx and sendTxBatch fall into a separate rate limit bucket
described below
, and are
linked to account type and staked tokens
.
REST API Endpoint Limits
The following limits apply to the
https://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/api/v1/
base URL, excluding
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
where different limits, listed
below
, apply. Different limits, also listed
below
, apply to
https://explorer.elliot.ai/api/
. To bypass IP-based rate limits, clients can authenticate each request so that only L1-based rate limits apply.
Builder accounts
Plus accounts
Premium/Advanced accounts

While standard accounts rate limits are not weighted, whenever
{premium_weighted_requests}/{endpoint_weight} < {standard_requests}
, the former limit is going to be applied. For example, both Standard and Premium/Advanced accounts will be able to make a maximum of 8 requests per rolling minute to the
changeAccountTier
endpoint.
You can apply for a Builder Account through our Discord support channel. It’s free of charge, but we reserve the right to review applications and verify the intended use. Builder Accounts include higher limits for querying our read-only REST API endpoints, excluding
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
; otherwise, standard account limits apply. Builders on this tier should authenticate every request, even when not explicitly required in our documentation.
WebSocket Limits
To prevent resource exhaustion, we enforce the following usage limits
per IP
:
Connections
: 255
Subscriptions per connection
: 500
Subscriptions per IP
: 5000
Unique Accounts per connection
: 500

: 5000

: 255 (not to be confused with channel subscriptions)
Max Messages Sent By Client Per Minute
: 200 (sendTx and sendBatchTx are
not
counted here, and follow the same limits as REST requests)
Max Inflight Messages
: 50 (sendTx and sendBatchTx are
not
counted here)
Deployments with no downtime might drop your connection, so it's recommended to have proper reconnection logic, in addition to ping/pong logic.
SendTx and SendTxBatch Limits (Premium/Advanced and Plus accounts)
The following limits apply to
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
requests, regardless of whether you send the requests using REST via HTTP, or via WebSocket. For these two types, we do not enforce IP limits, but only check rate limits at the L1 address level. Standard accounts are still bound to the 60 requests per minute limit. For rate limit purposes, fee credits count as staked LIT. For Premium/Advanced accounts,
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
are the only two types constrained by
Volume Quota
, necessary to create and modify orders.

L1Withdraw
(calling
withdraw()
on the Lighter contract) is an L1 transaction and is not subject to API rate limits.
Rate Limit Exceeding Behavior
If you exceed any rate limit:
You will receive
HTTP 429
, or
HTTP 405
For WebSocket connections, excessive messages may result in disconnection
When you're rate-limited on REST, WebSocket connections also get rate-limited, and vice versa
For Premium/Advanced and Plus accounts, mainnet endpoints fall into a separate bucket from
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
, meaning that getting rate-limited in one of the two buckets will not affect activity on the other. Put simply, sending too many transactions in a minute will not affect your ability to fetch data from the exchange, and vice versa.
To avoid this, please ensure your clients are implementing proper backoff and retry strategies.
Cooldown
Depending on whether you have been rate-limited by our firewall, or by the api servers, the cooldown period varies:
Firewall
: 60 seconds, static
Api servers
:
weightOfEndpoint/(totalWeight/60)
As an example, making a request to the

weight
of 300) after having exhausted your weighted requests in a given minute window, results in a 750ms cooldown period.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/timesta.title: Timestamps
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/timesta.content:
Read each timestamp in the context of its object. Lighter exposes block time, transaction execution time and message publication time, with units that vary by field.
Start with the object and the unit
Trade.timestamp
is block time in
milliseconds
.
Order.timestamp
is block time in
seconds
. A WebSocket envelope's
timestamp
is the API server's frame-generation time in
milliseconds
. None of these gives the time your order arrived at the API server.
Where the timestamps come from
The sequencer records a block timestamp when the block opens, before its first transaction. Trades in that block share this timestamp. Each transaction also has a finer-grained
transaction_time
, recorded in microseconds when it executes.
Sequencer
Block time appears as
Trade.timestamp
and
Tx.executed_at
in milliseconds, and as
Order.timestamp
in seconds. The order field reflects the block time of the order's last update.
transaction_time
records transaction execution time in microseconds.
last_updated_at
carries an aggregate of these execution timestamps for a market's order-book batch.
API server
envelope.timestamp
records frame-generation time in milliseconds on channels that expose it. The documented
trade
envelope has no publication timestamp. Record a local receive time if you need to track when it reaches your client.
Queue timing has a separate source, described below.
queued_at
uses the millisecond component of a Redis stream ID; a pending transaction can instead carry an API-server-time placeholder. Don't treat it as another sequencer timestamp.
Measure client latency on your own clock
Subtracting an API-server or Redis timestamp from a sequencer timestamp includes an unknown clock offset. For client-observed latency, use a local monotonic clock at submission and at the specific response or confirmation you want to measure. An acknowledgement and an execution confirmation measure different stages.
Seconds, milliseconds and microseconds
Choose the conversion by field and object. The service that supplies a value doesn't determine its unit.
Field
Native unit
Convert to milliseconds
Order.timestamp
seconds
value * 1_000
Trade.timestamp
,
Tx.executed_at
milliseconds
No conversion
envelope.timestamp
,
Tx.queued_at
milliseconds
No conversion
transaction_time
, book/ticker
last_updated_at
microseconds
value / 1_000
Python · field-specific conversions
Python
# Trade: retain integer microseconds for exact arithmetic.
block_us = trade["timestamp"] * 1_000
execution_us = trade["transaction_time"]
since_block_timestamp_us = execution_us - block_us

# Full Order objects use seconds for this particular field.
order_block_ms = order["timestamp"] * 1_000

# Tx.executed_at and envelope.timestamp are already milliseconds.
tx_block_ms = tx["executed_at"]
frame_ms = message["timestamp"]  # only if the envelope has this field
Integer division such as
transaction_time // 1_000
discards sub-millisecond precision. Treat an unavailable value such as
0
as missing timing data, rather than converting it into a date.

This table covers the fields and contexts listed here. Other time fields, including candle open times and expiry values, need their own definitions.
Block time and execution time
Reading a trade
Both timestamps inside a Trade come from the sequencer.
timestamp
records the block's opening time at millisecond resolution;
transaction_time
records that transaction's execution time at microsecond resolution.
For the trade in the public WebSocket example:
Event
Field
Value
Block opens
Trade.timestamp
1773854156654
ms
Transaction executes
transaction_time
1773854156686065
µs
The block timestamp also supplies
Tx.executed_at
. Other trades in the same block share the block time.
After conversion, the difference from the block timestamp is
32.065 ms
. This measures time relative to the block timestamp, with millisecond precision on the block side. It does not measure API ingress delay or client network latency.
trade/0 · abridged JSON
JSON
{
  "channel": "trade:0",
  "nonce": 8630448841,
  "trades": [{
    "trade_id": 16164557907,
    "market_id": 0,
    "size": "0.1336",
    "price": "2181.83",
    "block_height": 198321831,
    "timestamp": 1773854156654,
    "transaction_time": 1773854156686065
  }],
  "type": "update/trade"
}
For this block/execution pair, compare
timestamp * 1_000
with
transaction_time
. Don't compare the raw numbers in different units, or use timestamps as unique sequence identifiers.
No API ingress timestamp on a Trade
A trade does not expose the original request's arrival time. Liquidations, stop-loss/take-profit triggers and expiry cancellations can originate inside the sequencer; those internal actions don't pass through the API edge as client submissions.
The
trade
envelope has no publication timestamp in the public schema. A local arrival timestamp records when your client received the message; it cannot tell you when the server sent it.
Market data publication
On
order_book
and
ticker
, the outer
timestamp
records API-server frame generation. The
last_updated_at
value describes sequencer activity represented by the market's processed batch.
order_book/0 · abridged JSON
JSON
{
  "channel": "order_book:0",
  "last_updated_at": 1774884082309144,
  "offset": 1558300,
  "order_book": {
    "asks": [{ "price": "2064.54", "size": "0.3285" }],
    "bids": [],
    "nonce": 9182390020,
    "begin_nonce": 9182389998,
    "last_updated_at": 1774884082309144
  },
  "timestamp": 1774884082326,
  "type": "update/order_book"
}
The normalized numeric difference in this example is 16.856 ms. Because the two fields use different clocks, that number cannot isolate batching, serialization or network delay.
Envelope timestamps also appear on
market_stats
,
candle
,
user_stats
,
spot_market_stats
,
mark_price_candle
,
height
and
account_all_assets
. Check the schema of the channel you consume; not every envelope includes this field.
How book and ticker use last_updated_at
The standard
order_book
channel batches updates every 50 ms. The market cache takes the maximum
transaction_time
over every order changed in the processed batch, including changes away from the best bid or offer. Ticker reads that same stored value.
For example, suppose a market batch contains these order changes:
Underlying order change
Transaction execution time
Order A changes at the best bid
T + 1,000
µs
Order B changes deeper in the book
T + 8,000
µs
The stored market
last_updated_at
is
T + 8,000
µs. Order book and ticker both read this value for the corresponding market state, even though Order B is outside the best bid and offer.
Public price levels contain price and size, with no per-level
transaction_time
. The times above belong to the underlying order changes and illustrate the batch aggregation.
Compare book and ticker values for the corresponding nonce/state. Messages received next to each other may describe different updates, so arbitrary cross-channel pairs need not match.
Continuity and freshness are separate checks
For consecutive order-book updates, verify that
begin_nonce
equals the previous
nonce
. That detects missing updates; it doesn't establish how old the latest message is.
Track local time since the last received update for stream freshness. An envelope timestamp can help assess publication age if you account for client/server clock offset. Neither a recent frame nor a gap-free sequence alone proves that the underlying market state is recent.

REST endpoints and acknowledgements
recentTrades
and
trades
return Trade objects: their
timestamp
is block time in ms, while
transaction_time
uses µs. Full Order objects use seconds for
timestamp
.
orderBookOrders
returns
SimpleOrder
objects. This schema includes
transaction_time
, but neither
timestamp
nor
last_updated_at
.
Known limitation: orderBookOrders

is currently not populated and returns
0
. Treat this value as unavailable timing data; don't use it as an execution timestamp.
A successful submission response from
sendTx
or
sendTxBatch
acknowledges submission. The WebSocket send response can include a
tx_hash
and
predicted_execution_time_ms
; the prediction is not an actual execution timestamp.
Confirm the outcome you need
Check the transaction's status and result to establish execution. To establish a fill, check the trade record and the order's status and filled amounts. An executed order-placement or cancellation transaction can have a
transaction_time
without producing a fill.
Integration checklist
Map each timestamp to its object and unit. Convert seconds, milliseconds and microseconds explicitly.
Keep block time, transaction execution time, queue time and frame-generation time separate.
Use stream-specific sequence information for ordering and
begin_nonce
for book continuity. Track freshness separately.
Measure client latency with a local monotonic clock; don't infer server latency across different clocks.
Handle missing or zero timing values and confirm fills from execution results and trade/order data.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/trading.title: Signing Transactions
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/trading.content:
Traders can trade programmatically using the
sendTx
and
sendTxBatch
REST endpoints, or
json/sendTx
and
json/sendTxBatch
types via Websocket. Creating an API key is required to sign transactions.
📘
For the current binary options discovery methods and response models, use
lighter-sdk 1.1.8
or newer, or
lighter-go v1.0.12
or newer. Python 1.1.8 also fixes the
boPnl
authorization header. The standard create, modify and cancel order flow is unchanged; discover binary options market IDs through
events
.
The shared-library signer uses signed 64-bit market indices (
int64
). If you call it directly from C/C++ or a custom FFI binding, use a
.h
file and bindings that match your signer library. Update declarations that still use
int cMarketIndex
to
long long int cMarketIndex
, as shown in the
current signer header
.
See the
Python binary options examples
, especially
create_order_from_event.py
, for market discovery through
events
followed by
create_order
.
Orders that have the correct syntax will be accepted by the API servers, returning code=200. This does not guarantee the execution of your order, as the sequencer could still reject it if parameters are not set properly. To monitor orders execution, see
Confirming execution
.
Sign Transactions
Every
transaction
needs to be signed using the
SignerClient
. Using the
Python SDK
, you can initialize it as follows:
Python
client = lighter.SignerClient(  
        url=BASE_URL,  
        api_private_keys={API_KEY_INDEX:PRIVATE_KEY},  
        account_index=ACCOUNT_INDEX
    )
The code for the signer can be found in the same repo, in the
signer_client.py
file. You may notice that it uses a binary for the signer: the code for it can be found in the
lighter-go
public repo, and you can compile it yourself using the
justfile
.
The TypeScript examples on this page use the WASM signer from the
TypeScript quickstart
and this helper:
TypeScript
async function sendTx(tx: { txType: number; txInfo: string }) {
  const r = await fetch(`${BASE_URL}/api/v1/sendTx`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
    body: new URLSearchParams({ tx_type: String(tx.txType), tx_info: tx.txInfo }),
  }).then(r => r.json());
  if (r.code !== 200) throw new Error(`${r.code}: ${r.message}`);
  return r; // { tx_hash, predicted_execution_time_ms, volume_quota_remaining }
}
Every order carries a
nonce
and uses
integer prices and sizes
. Both are explained in
Core concepts
: see
Nonce
(including which rejected transactions consume a nonce) and
Integer prices and sizes
(including minimum order sizes).
📘
Binary options support limit and market orders only, with
reduceOnly = 0
and
triggerPrice = 0
. Up/Down markets use integer price ticks from
1
to
99
. Create and modify requests must be within the market's trading window and pass its frozen-book and price-cap checks. See
Binary options: Trading and fees
.

When cancelling, you may see

as an argument – you can use the same value. If

These are also defined in
signer_client.py
in the Python SDK, and in
constants.go
in the GO SDK.
Market order
TypeScript
// Buy 0.05 ETH, paying at most $3,150
const tx = check(lighter.SignCreateOrder(
  0, clientOrderIndex, toInt(0.05, 4), toInt(3150, 2),
  0,      // buy
  1,      // MARKET
  0,      // IOC
  0, 0,
  0,      // orderExpiry: 0 for IOC
  0, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  0, await nextNonce(), API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
await sendTx(tx);
Pick
price
from the order book with a slippage buffer (e.g. best ask × 1.01 for buys). If the book can't fill at that price or better, the rest is cancelled.
Post-only limit order
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignCreateOrder(
  0, clientOrderIndex, toInt(0.05, 4), toInt(2900, 2),
  0, 0 /* LIMIT */, 2 /* POST_ONLY */, 0, 0,
  Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 3600e3,
  0, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  0, await nextNonce(), API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
Stop-loss and take-profit
Set
triggerPrice
and
price
.
price
is the worst fill price once triggered, i.e. the allowed slippage, with the same logic as taker orders. Use
reduceOnly = 1
to protect a position.
To attach TP/SL to an entry in one go, use
SignCreateGroupedOrders
(OTO / OCO / OTOCO groupings). Grouped orders count as one transaction for quota. See
WASM signer functions
.
Modify
TypeScript
const tx = check(lighter.SignModifyOrder(
  marketIndex, clientOrderIndex, newBaseAmount, newPrice, newTriggerPrice,
  0, 0, 0,  // integrator fields (keep the same as the original order)
  0, 0,     // self-trade modes
  0, await nextNonce(),
  0,        // orderVersion: optional; if set, must be > current version
  API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX,
));
Order Version
You can specify an
order_version
when modifying orders, so that the sequencer will reject any version that is not strictly greater than the order's current stored version, returning
AppErrInvalidOrderOrderVersion
. This is optional, and examples can be found
here
(http) and
here
(ws). Order events will include
order_version
, and Trade events will include
ask_order_version
,
bid_order_version
.
Self-trade prevention
selfTradeBehaviorMode
and
selfTradeEqualityMode
control what happens when your order would match another order of yours. The default
0, 0
expires the resting (maker) order when both orders come from the same account index. Other values are listed in
Other order enums
.
🚧
Not combinable with partner fees
A non-default self-trade mode
can't be combined with non-zero integrator fees
on the same order (error
21159
). If you charge
partner fees
, leave both self-trade modes at
0
.
Cancel
TypeScript
// One order
lighter.SignCancelOrder(marketIndex, clientOrderIndex, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX);

// All orders (timeInForce 0 = now; cancelAllMarketIndex 255 = all markets)
lighter.SignCancelAllOrders(0, 0, 255, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX);
Batch
Send up to
50 transactions
in one request. All transactions in a batch must use the same account and API key, with consecutive nonces:
TypeScript
const n = await nextNonce();
const txs = [0, 1, 2].map(i => check(lighter.SignCreateOrder(/* … */ 0, n + i, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX)));

await fetch(`${BASE_URL}/api/v1/sendTxBatch`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    tx_types: JSON.stringify(txs.map(t => t.txType)),
    tx_infos: JSON.stringify(txs.map(t => t.txInfo)),
  }),
});
The whole batch waits for the
longest speed bump
of any transaction in it. Mixing a taker order into a batch of post-only orders delays all of them.
Large batches:
request-body size limits at the CDN edge can reject a large REST batch before it reaches the API (you'll get an HTTP error without Lighter's JSON body). REST batches of up to ~15 orders are safe. For bigger batches, use WebSocket
jsonapi/sendtxbatch
(
below
), which accepts messages up to 64 KB, enough for 50 orders.
Python example:
send_batch_tx_http.py
.
Leverage and margin
TypeScript
// Initial margin fraction in basis points of 10,000: 10x leverage -> 1000
lighter.SignUpdateLeverage(marketIndex, 1000, 0 /* 0 cross, 1 isolated */, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX);

// Add/remove isolated margin
lighter.SignUpdateMargin(marketIndex, usdcAmount, direction /* 1 add, 0 remove */, 0, nonce, API_KEY_INDEX, ACCOUNT_INDEX);
Sending over WebSocket
Lower latency than REST, same limits:
JSON
{ "type": "jsonapi/sendtx", "data": { "id": "my-req-1", "tx_type": 14, "tx_info": { … } } }
jsonapi/sendtxbatch
takes
tx_types
and
tx_infos
arrays (max 50). Messages are limited to
64 KB
after decompression.
permessage-deflate
is supported, but it doesn't raise that limit. Full message format:
Send Tx
and
Send Batch Tx
.
Confirming execution
sendTx
returning
code: 200
only means the transaction was accepted. Subscribe to
account_orders/{market}/{account}
or
account_tx/{account}
to see fills and rejections. See
Account data & positions
.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/trouble.content:
Error codes and their names are listed in
Data Structures, Constants and Errors
. This page covers what usually causes them.
📘
For the current binary options discovery methods and response models, use
lighter-sdk 1.1.8
or newer, or
lighter-go v1.0.12
or newer. Python 1.1.8 also fixes the
boPnl
authorization header. The standard create, modify and cancel order flow is unchanged; discover binary options market IDs through
events
.
The shared-library signer uses signed 64-bit market indices (
int64
). If you call it directly from C/C++ or a custom FFI binding, use a
.h
file and bindings that match your signer library. Update declarations that still use
int cMarketIndex
to
long long int cMarketIndex
, as shown in the
current signer header
.
See the
Python binary options examples
, especially
create_order_from_event.py
, for market discovery through
events
followed by
create_order
.
sendTx
returned 200 but my order isn't there
200
means the API accepted the transaction. The sequencer can still reject it, for example because of a price outside the allowed band, a taker order that can't fill at your worst price, or insufficient margin for a taker order. Check
account_tx/{account}
on WebSocket or
GET /api/v1/tx?by=hash&value=<tx_hash>
.
invalid nonce
(21104)
Two processes are using the same API key concurrently. Use one key per process, or serialize.
A previous tx failed in the sequencer
without
consuming its nonce (e.g.
ExpiredAt
passed, not enough margin for a resting order), so the later nonces you already sent are now one step ahead and fail too. Refetch
nextNonce
and re-sign. See
When a rejected transaction consumes its nonce
.
Batch nonces must be consecutive (21105).
invalid PublicKey, please run changePubKey
(21108) / key check fails
The key at that
apiKeyIndex
isn't registered for that
accountIndex
, or it was replaced by another app using the same index. Register it again (
Create accounts programmatically
).
Signature rejected / wrong chain
The
chainId
in
CreateClient
must be
304
for mainnet and
300
for testnet. See
Environments & endpoints
.
Order size or price is off by powers of ten
You mixed up decimals.
base_amount = size × 10^size_decimals
,
price = price × 10^price_decimals
, taken from
orderBookDetails
for
that
perps or spot market, or from
events
for binary options. If you use
lighter-ts
, also watch the display/real
multiplier
(see
Market data
).
Order rejected as too small
Below
min_base_amount
or
min_quote_amount
(the larger applies). For binary options, the minimum quote check uses
P × size
for both buy and sell orders, where
P
is the Up price. A Down order can fail this check even when its
(1 − P) × size
cost exceeds the minimum. See
Binary options order rules
.
Binary options create or modify rejected
Code
Check
21631
The transaction's block time must fall within the market's
start_timestamp
–
end_timestamp
. Refresh
events
and select a market whose trading window is open
21632
Use a price below
settlement_cap
; for Up/Down this means integer ticks
1
–
99
, not
100
21638
The operator has frozen the order book; check
is_frozen
before retrying
These checks apply to both
CreateOrder
and
ModifyOrder
. See
Binary options: Trading and fees
.
Integrator fee rejected
The client is on Standard, the fee exceeds the approved max, the approval expired, or the client already has 4 partners. See
Partner Attribution
.
HTTP 429 / 405
Rate limited. Back off, authenticate requests, reduce polling (use WebSocket), or change tier. See
Rate Limits
.
WebSocket disconnects
No frame within 2 minutes, too many subscriptions, reading too slowly, or a server deployment. Send pings every ~60 s and reconnect automatically.
account not found
(21100) after a deposit
Deposits take a few minutes to credit (CCTP: ~15–20 min). Poll
accountsByL1Address
, or check UDA status.
WASM:
argument N is undefined
/
expects N args
Every positional argument is required. Pass
0
for unused ones. Check the order in
WASM signer functions
.
Still stuck?
Open a ticket in
#support
on
Discord
with the
tx_hash
, account index, API key index and the full response.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/use-wit.title: Use these docs with AI
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/use-wit.content:
These docs are designed to be read by AI assistants and coding agents as well as people.
llms.txt
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/llms.txt
lists every guide and API endpoint with a one-line summary and a link to its Markdown version. Point your agent at it to discover pages.
Markdown pages
Add
.md
to any page URL to get clean Markdown:
Text
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/quickstart-typescript.md
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/reference/sendtx.md
Tell your agent how to build on Lighter
Drop the
Agent instructions
into your repo as
AGENTS.md
/
CLAUDE.md
/
.cursor/rules
so your coding agent follows Lighter's rules (decimals, nonces, key safety) by default.
Devin
Commit the
Agent instructions
as
AGENTS.md
in the root of the repo Devin works on. Devin reads it automatically at the start of every session.
Optionally, add a
skill
for Lighter work at
.agents/skills/lighter/SKILL.md
, so Devin looks up the docs before writing Lighter code:
.agents/skills/lighter/SKILL.md
---
name: lighter
description: Use when writing or changing code that calls the Lighter API, WebSocket or signer.
---

1. Read https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/llms.txt and open the relevant pages (append .md to any page URL).
2. Follow the rules in AGENTS.md: integer prices and sizes, per-API-key nonces, confirm execution after sendTx.
3. Test against testnet (https://testnet.zklighter.elliot.ai, chain ID 300) before touching mainnet.
Letting an AI agent trade
If you're building an agent that trades on a user's behalf:
Give it a
dedicated API key
on a
dedicated sub-account
funded with only what it may risk.
Use a
read-only token
for any agent that only needs to look. See
Read-only Authentication
.
Never give an agent the user's Ethereum private key. API keys can't send funds to other owners.
Keep a human confirmation step for withdrawals, transfers and large orders.

https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/volume-.title: Volume Quota
https://apidocs.lighter.xyz/docs/volume-.content:
Volume Quota
gives users higher rate limits on
SendTx
and
SendTxBatch
based on trading volume and is
only enforced for Plus and Premium/Advanced accounts
. The only types of transactions that consume volume quota are:
L2CreateOrder
(14)
L2CancelAllOrders
(16)
L2ModifyOrder
(17)
L2CreateGroupedOrders
(28)
Other types of transactions has separate rate limits, see
Transaction Type Limits
.
For more details on transaction types, see
constants.go
. Grouped orders only consume one quota. Cancels do not consume quota. If you include
n
transactions in a
SendTxBatch
request,
n
quota will be consumed.
For every 2 USD of trading volume, traders receive an additional transaction limit (i.e. volume quota increases by 1).
SendTx
and
SendTxBatch
requests will return a response indicating the remaining quota, e.g. "10780 volume quota remaining.". Every 15 seconds, you get a free
SendTx
which won't consume volume quota (nor show remaining quota). Volume quota is shared across all sub-accounts under the same L1 address.
New accounts start at 1K quota, and you can stack at most 15.000.000 TX allowance in your volume quota, which does not expire.
This differs from Rate Limits, which enforce a maximum of
72000
transactions per minute for Premium/Advanced accounts. You can check the weight of the endpoints, and standard accounts limits here:
Rate Limits
.

,

"Same owner" means both accounts belong to the same master account, i.e. the same master account and its sub-accounts.
Transaction
L1 signature required
Not required

Always

Transfer
Sender and receiver have
different
owners. This includes
fast withdrawals

Transfers between the same owner's accounts (e.g. master to sub-account)

Integrator has a
different
owner
and
at least one max fee is > 0
Zero-fee approvals and revokes; approving an account with the same owner
Everything else (orders,
Withdraw
, …)
Never;
messageToSign
isn't returned

Connection
URL:
wss://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream
;
wss://testnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream
You can directly connect to the WebSocket server using wscat:
Shell
wscat -c 'wss://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream'
If you're connecting from a restricted region, you can still access read-only data:
Shell
wscat -c 'wss://mainnet.zklighter.elliot.ai/stream?readonly=true'
Keepalive Requirements
Clients are responsible for keeping the connection alive by sending at least one frame every
2 minutes
. This can be either:
A
WebSocket ping frame
Any application-level message
Clients sending
{"type":"ping"}
will receive back
{"type":"pong"}
.
If the server receives no frames from a client within the 2-minute window, it will close the connection.
Support for
permessage-deflate
compression is enabled.
Clients that fall behind on reading messages may be disconnected more aggressively than before.
Send Tx
You can send transactions using the websocket as follows:
JSON
{
    "type": "jsonapi/sendtx",
    "data": {
        "id": STRING, // returned in the ws response
        "tx_type": INTEGER,
        "tx_info": ...
    }
}
The
tx_type
options can be found in the
SignerClient
file, while
tx_info
can be generated using the sign methods in the SignerClient.
Example:
ws_send_tx.py
Send Batch Tx
You can send batch transactions to execute up to 15 transactions in a single message.
JSON
{
    "type": "jsonapi/sendtxbatch",
    "data": {
        "id": STRING, // returned in the ws response
        "tx_types": "[INTEGER]",
        "tx_infos": "[tx_info]"
    }
}
The
tx_type
options can be found in the
SignerClient
file, while
tx_info
can be generated using the sign methods in the SignerClient.
Example:
ws_send_batch_tx.py

The order book channel sends the new ask and bid orders for the given market in batches, every 50ms. While the nonce is tied to Lighter's matching engine, the offset is tied to the API servers; hence, you can expect the offset to change drastically on reconnection if you're routed to a different server. Candlesticks
Real-time candlestick (OHLCV) updates via WebSocket. Subscribe to any market and resolution to receive live candle data as trades occur. Supported resolutions:
1m
,
5m
,
15m
,
30m
,
1h
,
4h
,
12h
,
1d
. The candles[] array allows up to 2 candles to be sent in a single update when a candle period closes (rolls over). If so, candles[0] will be the oldest, just closed candle.
JSON
{
	"type": "subscribe",
	"channel": "candle/{market_id}/{resolution}"
}
Example Subscription
JSON
{
	"type": "subscribe",
	"channel": "candle/0/1m"
}
Response Structure (Subscribe)
JSON
{
  "type": "subscribed/candle",
  "channel": "candle:{market_id}:{resolution}",
  "timestamp": INTEGER, 
  "candles": [
    {
      "t": INTEGER, // candle open timestamp
      "o": FLOAT, // open price
      "h": FLOAT, // high price
      "l": FLOAT, // low price
      "c": FLOAT, // close price
      "v": FLOAT, // base token volume
      "V": FLOAT, // quote token volume
      "i": INTEGER // last trade id
    }
  ]
}
Response Structure (Updates)
JSON
{
  "type": "update/candle",
  "channel": "candle:{market_id}:{resolution}",
  "timestamp": INTEGER,
  "candles": [
    {
      "t": INTEGER,
      "o": FLOAT,
      "h": FLOAT,
      "l": FLOAT,
      "c": FLOAT,
      "v": FLOAT,
      "V": FLOAT,
      "i": INTEGER
    }
  ]
}

Average Entry Prices
Updates on the
account_spot_avg_entry_prices
channel are triggered whenever an event occurs for a given spot asset. Each event is accounted for as a buy or sell executed at the index price. Events include trades, deposits, withdrawals, transfers, and staking. The
last_trade_id
field confirms the validity of the data returned up to that
trade_id
.
JSON
{
    "type": "subscribe",
    "channel": "account_spot_avg_entry_prices/{ACCOUNT_ID}",
    "auth": "{AUTH_TOKEN}"
}

{
    "type": "subscribe",
    "channel": "account_spot_avg_entry_prices/1234",

Request for Quote (RFQ)
This channel allows you to receive all currently open RFQs, followed by live updates as new ones arrive. RFQ responses are hidden if you're not the requester, so you will only see the market and its size. API endpoints to create, respond, update, get, and list RFQs are available
here
. Currently, this program is whitelist-only.

{
	"type": "subscribe", 
	"channel": "rfq", 
	"auth": "{AUTH_TOKEN}"
}
